主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-11-16

Bringing physics-based controller policies to virtual reality

Abstract

The use of physics-based controllers in video games and virtual reality (VR) is now technically possible, but little attention has been paid to evaluating the movement quality generated by such controllers, particularly when high-quality motions are needed. Moreover, these controllers have been developed in research-oriented physics engines, which are not suitable for production projects, where game engines like Unity3D or Unreal Engine are preferred. Nowadays, it is easy to set up any element of a VR experience so users can interact with it physically, except for interactive VR characters. Can we extend this to animated VR characters?

In this work, we studied whether physics-based character animation (PBCA) controllers can produce high-quality movement in VR-compatible environments (Unity3D, WebXR). Since VR experiences typically use rigged and textured characters, we evaluated the quality of the movement by capturing and manually retargeting eight walking styles to two rigged and textured characters, which served as reference animations for comparison with the motions generated by the PBCA controllers. We also found that showing the training results on rigged and textured characters helped highlight the controller policies’ animation inaccuracies.

We evaluated the quality of the results, as well as the losses at each stage of the processing pipeline: data ingest, training and inference. For data ingest, we computed accuracy metrics related to the retargeting method used. For training, we computed accuracy metrics related to different training policies and different training environments. We developed new JAX implementations of state-of-the-art PBCA controllers (DeepMimic, AMP and ADD) which can be trained in MuJoCo-MJX in minutes, 50 times faster than in a traditional CPU-based training environment. The benefit of these particular implementations is that the resulting control policies can be readily transferred to Unity3D and support cross-platform compilation, including Android, something critical for use in VR production. For inference, we tested these controller policies in Unity3D and WebXR. Our results suggest that DeepMimic and ADD trained in MuJoCo-MJX generate controller policies with better animation fidelity than other methods.

To simplify the comparison between controller policies, and different reference animations, we implemented an animation fidelity index (afi). Its results are analogous to other more common metrics, but afi is more intuitive to interpret and thus simplifies the comparison of training methods across the successive stages of the processing pipeline. We also did an expert comparison between the reference motions and the end result.

Our results suggest that any use of PBCA in production projects should be approached with caution. Some inaccuracies readily visible to an animator were difficult to detect with the different metrics commonly used, and the overall quality of the results varied considerably depending on different choices made across the processing and delivery pipeline. Finally, we provide the animation data and code to facilitate the transfer of physics-based control research results to the artistic and production communities.

Since DeepMimic [22] and DReCon [3] demonstrated that physics-based controllers driven by Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies can learn to mimic reference motion capture clips, a critical question remained underexplored: can we use physics-based controller policies to drive virtual reality (VR) characters? The answer seems to be sometimes, but unfortunately not if we want to closely match high-quality reference animations.

The lack of a standard integration of research-oriented physics engines into production-oriented game engines remains a barrier. It is also necessary to check the movement quality generated by the controller policies at each stage of the pipeline to transfer the controllers in a production environment. This can partially be done with objective metrics, but it is also necessary to rely on the expertise of an animation specialist.

In character animation, the movement is the means of expression, and any degradation in fidelity directly undermines the artistic intent. However, most evaluations focus on task success—survival rate, tracking reward, perturbation recovery— and rarely measure the fine-grained animation quality that determines production readiness. Moreover, results are typically demonstrated in research simulators rather than in production game engines (e.g., Unity3D, Unreal Engine) where animation content is actually deployed.

In this work, we implemented an end-to-end pipeline to train controller policies from an animated character, and a systematic evaluation of animation fidelity at different stages of the pipeline. Following the trends in the Physics-based character animation (PBCA) community, our pipeline trained on GPU, which is much faster than CPU training. However, to meet the requirements of production deployments, the inference was done on the CPU in VR-compatible environments (Unity3D, WebXR). We evaluated the quality of the outcome of three physics-based controller policies (DeepMimic[21], AMP[24], ADD[38]), and compared it with the outcome of a simpler and slower CPU-based training pipeline.

To assess the flexibility and reliability of different controller policies, we tested each of them on two characters and eight walking styles. We chose walking reference animations because they should be relatively easy for a PBCA policy to learn. This allowed us to focus our evaluation on animation quality, something critical for the adoption of these techniques in a production context. In summary, our contributions are:

  • 1.

    A GPU-accelerated pipeline with JAX implementations of state-of-the-art PBCA controller policies (DeepMimic, AMP, and ADD). From an FBX animation file, this pipeline trained a policy in minutes on a single GPU, converted it to ONNX and integrated it into a Unity3D scene, ready for cross-platform deployment, including Android-based VR headsets. We also deployed the controller policies on a VR-compatible web environment based on WebXR.

  • 2.

    A high-quality animation benchmark comprising two rigged and textured characters of different body proportions (adult male and female child), each performing eight walking styles, with reference motions manually retargeted to the characters by a professional animator.

  • 3.

    An evaluation of animation fidelity losses for different policies, each trained on different reference animations. We evaluated animation fidelity across all stages, from the source animation through training and to the final deployed controller policy. This was done with commonly used metrics, as well as with a new animation fidelity index, and visual inspection of each animation-policy pair. We also compared the policies with the outcome of an earlier CPU-based training pipeline that is also VR-compatible.

    • 1 Background

    1.1 Physics engines for VR production

    The two most popular game engines on the market are currently Unity3D111 https://unity.com/ and Unreal Engine222 https://www.unrealengine.com, which have considerably democratized video game and VR production. These game engines provide integrated physics engines (PhysX and Chaos for Unity3D and UE5, respectively) to simulate behaviours of physical entities. While their capabilities are suitable for many use cases, they were not designed to meet the needs of solving optimal control problems. They provide limited access to the physics engine API, and they are not compatible with modern training pipelines that are based on GPU-accelerated physical simulations integrated in the deep learning training stack. Moreover, research-oriented engines (MuJoCo333 https://mujoco.org/, Bullet444 https://github.com/bulletphysics/bullet3, DART555 https://dartsim.github.io/) and production game engines differ in their collision handling and numerical precision, and the extent to which policies trained in one physics engine can transfer to another remains unclear. We therefore choose to take advantage of the MuJoCo plugin for Unity3D, which allows evaluating and comparing our two training pipelines inside the same development environment.

    WebXR allows for the rendering of interactive VR environments in web browsers and is emerging as an alternative to traditional game engines for VR development. We also evaluate how it holds up against a standalone VR build.

    1.2 Humanoid controllers

    Humanoid controllers broadly divide into tracking-based controllers, which combine a kinematic motion planner with a physics-based controller trained to imitate the poses generated by the kinematic motion planner, and sensorimotor controllers, where the policy directly maps perceptions to motor actions through reward-driven learning [17].

    1.2.1 Tracking-based controllers

    Tracking-based controllers can produce high-quality animation by blending pre-recorded clips at runtime. However, the interaction with the environment is driven by the kinematic poses that the physical controller is trained to imitate, and they therefore lack physical interaction with the environment. DReCon [3] combines a physics-based controller with a kinematic motion planner [5, 13]. At inference time, the trained policy receives both the current physics state and a kinematic reference pose, and outputs joint torques that track the sequence of kinematic poses while maintaining balance.
    While simplifying the training process, this method involves additional computational overhead at inference time due to the need for kinematic motion synthesis and to provide an expanded observation space.

    1.2.2 Sensorimotor controllers with explicit rewards

    DeepMimic [22] demonstrated that carefully designed tracking rewards—exponentially weighted errors on joint positions, velocities, center of mass, and end-effectors—enable RL policies to imitate reference motions. This approach produces high fidelity on single clips but requires per-component reward tuning and explicit tracking of the animation clip’s phase (from 0 to 1) at inference time. VMP [28] extends explicit rewards to multi-motion settings by decoupling motion understanding (a pre-trained Variational Autoencoder on short motion windows) from physics control (a conditional RL policy), achieving stable convergence on 11 hours of diverse motion data. AMOR [1] further extends this by training a single multi-objective policy conditioned on reward weight vectors, enabling post-training trade-off tuning. The Disney Research robotics pipeline [8] similarly relies on DeepMimic-style rewards for production deployment of bipedal character robots, confirming that explicit rewards remain the preferred approach when animation fidelity is the priority.

    1.2.3 Sensorimotor controllers with adversarial rewards

    AMP [25] replaces hand-crafted tracking rewards with a learned discriminator that distinguishes reference motion transitions from policy-generated ones, using a GAIL-style adversarial objective. This eliminates reward engineering and captures stylistic features that are hard to specify analytically. Subsequent extensions include ASE [23] (reusable skill embeddings), CALM [32] (conditional latent models), and ReGAIL [4] (relative features for single-motion GAIL). ADD [38] modifies the discriminator to operate on displacement vectors between reference and agent states, using the zero vector as the only positive sample. MimicKit [26] provides a unified framework implementing DeepMimic, AMP, and ADD for fair comparison. A recent survey [15] systematically compares feature-based and GAN-based approaches, concluding that explicit tracking rewards excel at high-fidelity single-motion imitation while adversarial methods offer better scalability but suffer from training instability and coarser reward signals.

    1.2.4 Scaling and universal controllers

    PHC [19] uses progressive training and residual forces for robust multi-motion control. PULSE [18] learns a universal 32-dimensional motion latent space from the AMASS dataset. SuperPADL [14] scales to 5000+ skills via progressive distillation. SONIC [20] demonstrates that scaling data (100M+ frames), compute, and model size all improve motion tracking quality. BeyondMimic [16] achieves state-of-the-art tracking with unified hyperparameters across highly dynamic motions. CLoSD [33] combines a diffusion-based motion planner with a physics-based tracker in a closed feedback loop. Recent contributions have scaled these approaches to thousands of motions [14, 20, 34], enabled universal controllers [18, 16], and transferred policies to physical robots [8, 11].

    1.3 Animation fidelity metrics

    Despite rapid progress in controller capabilities, quantitative evaluation of animation quality remains inconsistent across the literature. Most papers report task-level metrics (survival rate, tracking reward, success percentage) rather than fine-grained fidelity measures. Common metrics include joint position mean average error (MAE) in degrees [28], end-effector position error in meters [21], or motion success rate [18].

    The recent tracking literature (VMP [28], CALM [32], BDX [8] and ASAP [11]) generally show a small set of metrics that allow comparing the methods: joint Mean Average Error (MAE) (in degrees or radians), root-relative Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) (mm), end-effector MAE (m), e(n) (m/frame), and success rate (% of episodes that survive a fixed rollout horizon).

    Perceptual studies have partially identified what the important factors are to judge pose similarity. The set of quaternions defining a pose for a given skeleton is not considered a good measure of perceived pose similarity [30]. Indeed, even minor deviations early in the kinematic chain will lead to obvious deviations in the end effectors. Furthermore, the angular distance between the pose joints is unable to capture deviations in higher-order kinematics that affect both visual fidelity and stability. The use of angular velocity for motion prediction seems more appropriate than the combination of pose and linear velocity [10]. It is also easier to interpret than other proposed metrics, such as Neural Pose Spectrum Similarity (NPSS) [7]. The physical meaning is more intuitive, and it can more easily be visualised in a graph to compare a reference animation and movement produced by a controller. For end-effectors, Euclidean distance has also been shown to matter, particularly for hands and fingers [9, 2].

    2 Materials and Methods

    2.1 Reference Data

    In most of the literature on physics-based controllers, motion retargeting is performed automatically. This is practical, but difficult to reconcile with high animation quality. Our experience, further confirmed by the results presented below, suggests that manual retargeting performed by a skilled animator, combined with a ragdoll matching the proportions of the reference skeleton, is what introduces a smaller fidelity loss. This is consistent with the production pipeline in [8], where artist-created reference motions are used to ensure animation quality in deployed robotic characters. Investing in manual retargeting, rather than relying on automated solutions, appears to be a sensible choice.

    To build a controlled, high-quality dataset and allow testing the extent to which the training pipeline works for characters of different proportions, we recruited two volunteers —a 10-year-old girl (LL) and a 35-year-old man (MM)— and instructed them to walk straight ahead in 8 different styles such as “neutral”, “angry” and “wounded” (see list in Table 2). The motion was recorded using a Vicon MX T-Series motion capture system (Vicon, Oxford Metrics, UK) consisting of 24 cameras (24 × T40S) sampling at 120 Hz. Vicon Shogun version 1.18 was used to generate a skeleton matching the actors’ proportions to automatically transfer each captured take to the target skeleton.

    We then transferred the animation data to rigged and textured characters, in three steps. First, a technical artist created a textured character model in Character Creator version 4 (one character per actor). Second, the Shogun skeleton was adapted using Blender to be compatible with Unity3D’s Humanoid definition— the number of bones in the spine was reduced from four to three to match the Humanoid layout, while preserving the actors’ segment lengths found in the Shogun reference, and each character skin was rigged onto this adapted skeleton.

    Third, a professional 3D animator used Motion Builder version 2026 to retarget each captured take from the Shogun skeleton onto the Unity3D-compatible skeleton and to clean the result. Since the motion-capture rig used a 3-finger marker setup that does not resolve every finger joint, the animator manually set each hand to a natural rest pose; no other body-part data was edited. Each take was then trimmed to an animation cycle of four footsteps. The final animation files used to train the physics-based controllers are in the supplementary materials.

    2.2 Training

    We used two different training pipelines, playground and modular-agents.

    2.2.1 Playground

    The main training pipeline used MJX [36], a JAX-compiled version of MuJoCo that runs entirely on GPUs. The RL policy used was PPO, implemented using the Brax training library [6], with 4096 parallel environments per training run. The control policies trained were JAX reimplementations of DeepMimic, AMP, and ADD. Policies were exported as ONNX models and loaded in Unity3D via the ONNX Runtime plugin. The main motivation for this training pipeline was to use modern hardware acceleration, as adopted in many recent papers on physics-based controllers [36, 6, 28, 20], which yielded at least an order of magnitude in training speed. This also enabled the adoption of the kind of massively parallelized training strategies recently demonstrated on motion-imitation benchmarks [19, 31, 20].

    This strategy introduced an additional challenge: the MJX (GPU) and MuJoCo C implementations differ in their collision handling and numerical precision, introducing a sim-to-sim transfer gap analogous to the sim-to-real gap in robotics [11, 29]. We minimized this gap through two strategies: (a) careful observation design—we excluded simulator-specific quantities such as composite inertia tensors (cinert) from the policy observations, as these differ between MJX and MuJoCo C and neural networks are sensitive even to small discrepancies, and (b) three-way validation comparing the policy output in the MJX training environment, in MuJoCo C and in Unity3D, flagging any experiment where cross-platform metrics diverged beyond 2σ.

    To systematically compare different characters and animations, we developed an automated pipeline that created the entire training dataset---MJCF ragdoll, reference joint trajectories, and animation metadata---directly from the FBX animation file using inverse kinematics retargeting.666 https://github.com/kevinzakka/mink

    2.2.2 Modular agents

    For comparison, we used the modular-agents training pipeline. This pipeline is based on extensions of ML-Agents in Unity3D. For training it uses MuJoCo compiled for CPU (MuJoCo C) and integrated in a plugin for Unity3D. The RL policy used was Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [27], in particular the implementation available in the ML-Agents package (version 4.0.0)777 https://github.com/unity-technologies/ml-agents. The training scene was implemented in Unity3D version 6.3.3f1, using a custom library developed to generate the training events and the RL signals (observations, rewards, actuators), which is publicly available [12]. The training environment was generated by compiling a Linux binary of the Unity3D scene, communicating with the ML-Agents Python training package over a client-server socket. The control policies used for training were C# reimplementations of the DReCon and DeepMimic rewards and observations, adapted to a Unity3D environment. Further details on the training software architecture are provided in section A of the supplementary materials.

    2.3 Evaluation of the controller policies

    2.3.1 Training strategy

    To find common ground for both pipelines, we chose to do all training with simulation steps every 0.008 s (125Hz), and up to 100M simulation steps. This took approximately 40 hours for each training run based on modular-agents, and 40 minutes for each training run based on playground. All playground training runs were performed on an Intel Core i9-14900K, 64 GB of RAM, and two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 graphics cards. All modular-agents training runs were done either on a Windows 11 Pro with an Intel Core i9-14900K, 64 GB of RAM, and a NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super graphics card, or a Windows 11 Pro with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X and 128 GB of RAM. The configuration files, including the environment and PPO hyperparameters, can be found in the supplementary materials.

    2.3.2 How to compare different controller policies in VR

    Practical validation of the method included compilation for different platforms (Windows, Linux, MacOS, Android) to confirm the models could be used in production projects. Since Android builds are not included in MuJoCo releases, we recompiled the physics engine from its source to integrate it into VR builds. We also compared these builds with running the entire environment in a web browser.

    To compare the movement quality, independently of the controller policy used and the delivery method (Unity3D, WebXR), we recorded the movement data generated by the controller for exactly one animation loop, with no perturbations. We analysed the data with a set of custom Python scripts (which we provide in the supplementary materials). This allowed us to compare different training pipelines and controllers in the same context.

    2.3.3 How to compare different pipeline stages

    To compare the motion generated by different policies with the reference animation used for training the policies, we used metrics with patterns that are easy to identify. For example, Figure 1 shows the end-effector distance to the root for one reference animation, across five policies. In a walking pattern, the maxima and minima of this distance in the foot should be very well aligned with the reference animation.

    To compare between policies, and between policies trained with different reference animations, we found that the measures common in PBCA literature did not seem to consider the perceptual studies on the topic (see section 1.3). We therefore complemented the standard metrics with an animation fidelity index. Specifically, we considered three factors, with equal weight:

  • 1.

    Instantaneous angular celerity, i.e., the magnitude of the angular velocity (one ℝ value per joint)

  • 2.

    Instantaneous linear celerity of end-effectors (hands, feet) relative to the root (4×ℝ values per character)

  • 3.

    Instantaneous linear celerity of the root, to reflect the displacement, independently of the forward direction ( one ℝ value per character)

    • To derive a compact index from these metrics, we built a per-frame signal vector for each sequence and computed the cross-correlation between two sequences of poses—generated either by a reference animation or by a physics-based controller. Our animation fidelity index afi was defined as the weighted sum of these:

    afi=1/3*((∑ₙ₌₀^Lr_ref(n)r_phy(n+m))/(∥r_ref∥²∥r_phy∥²)(1)
    +(∑ₙ₌₀^La_ref(n)a_phy(n+m))/(∥a_ref∥²∥a_phy∥²)(2)
    +(∑ₙ₌₀^Le_ref(n)e_phy(n+m))/(∥e_ref∥²∥e_phy∥²))(3)

    where:

  • r(n)

    is the root linear celerity(1 ℝ).

  • a(n)

    is the angular celerity for all joints (19 ℝ).

  • e(n)

    is the celerity for end-effectors relative to the root (4 ℝ).

  • ref

    indicates the poses from the animation.

  • phy

    indicates the poses from the physical controller.

  • L

    indicates the temporal length of the animation.

  • m=0

    because we assume signals are temporally aligned.


    • The afi is composed of three sub-indices. Term (1) reflects differences in speed of global movement. Term (2) reflects differences in the magnitude of angular velocities. Term in (3) reflects differences in the magnitude of end-effector velocities, relative to the root of the skeleton. To further illustrate the evaluation methodology, Figure 2 shows the metrics contributing to the afi for the “Happy” walk of character “LL”, trained in playground with the DeepMimic policy.

    This index is inspired by perceptual studies (see section 1.3): it is based on angular velocities, it takes into account the importance of the end-effectors and root displacement, it does not compare pose rotations, and it is indifferent to the direction of the movement.

    It is also universal, in the sense that it does not impose any constraint on physical contacts, or animation duration. Therefore, even if here we focus on walking motions, it should also work for other tasks such as jumps, rolls, or grabbing objects. Moreover, since the per-joint angular celerity, the end-effector relative celerities, and the root linear celerity are non-negative by construction, the afi stays within [0,1], thus facilitating an intuitive interpretation as a similarity score. We therefore use this metric as a convenient way to monitor the quality of the behavior generated by the controllers at different stages.

    3 Results

    3.1 Training results

    All controllers evaluated achieve 100% survival, both in Unity3D and WebXR, across all 16 motions. In Table 1, we show these metrics for our three playground controller policies. ADD produced movement with scores very close to DeepMimic trained in playground. We believe ADD gives better afi scores than AMP because the displacement-based discriminator provides a more direct tracking signal. These findings were unexpected, as we anticipated that the results would align with the broader pattern observed in the literature: explicit tracking rewards [22, 28, 8] consistently produce higher single-motion fidelity than adversarial approaches [25], a trade-off also highlighted by Li et al. [15]. Our results suggest that, while the two are not equivalent, the difference for ADD is relatively small.

    Adversarial methods (AMP, ADD) offer practical advantages—no per-component reward tuning, implicit style capture, more controller flexibility—but at a measurable fidelity cost. ADD narrows this gap substantially compared to AMP, but DeepMimic remains uniformly superior; for production scenarios requiring faithful reproduction of specific motions, the use of explicit rewards like in DeepMimic remains the most reliable approach. However, when several animations need to be combined more flexibly, ADD seems to provide a viable option.

    In ADD[37], the discriminator saturates rapidly (reaching near-100% accuracy within 20M steps, since the zero-displacement positive sample is trivially separable), after which the style reward gradient vanishes. We emphasize that this saturation is a fundamental architectural limitation of the displacement-based formulation, not a tuning problem: the discriminator’s positive class is a single point (the zero vector), which is trivially separable from any non-zero displacement distribution regardless of network capacity, regularization, or training schedule. A small hybrid task reward component (5–15% weight) resolves this by maintaining gradient flow after discriminator saturation. With this fix, all 16 motions achieved 100% survival in Unity3D and WebXR deployment.

    afi gives the same results as the joint-space (MAE) and Cartesian (MPJPE) metrics on the overall ranking: DeepMimic is the strongest tracker on both skeletons, ADD is the second-best, and AMP trails on every column. The two metric families are complementary. MAE and MPJPE are pose-error metrics computed at the same frame index: they answer “how far is the agent’s pose from the reference’s pose at time t” and are easy to inflate by a small phase shift, even when the trajectories are otherwise faithful. afi is a time-aware cross-correlation of velocity and end-effector trajectories: it tolerates small phase shifts but penalises wrong overall pacing, missing follow-through, and jitter. NPSS, the frequency-domain reference metric, gives similar results, but it can sometimes be challenging because ADD rollouts that terminate early concentrate spectral power at f→0 – the same low-frequency band some animation occupies.

    3.2 Losses in Animation Fidelity

    To better understand where animation fidelity is lost, Figure 3 shows the afi at each stage of the playground pipeline (MJX → MuJoCo C → Unity3D), across animations. For comparison, we also show the losses in the modular-agents pipeline.

  • 1.

    Motion retargeting. Virtually all methods for training physical controllers with reference motion data use a retargeting strategy to map kinematic poses, defined as instantaneous rotations of a reference skeleton, to a targeted ragdoll. This step defines the targeted rotations and angular velocities in a reduced space defined by the humanoid’s articulations. To minimize the loss of accuracy of this step, we manually retargeted the captured animations to the reference characters and made the ragdolls match the proportions of the character skeletons as closely as possible. However, in both pipelines, there is minimal retargeting, from the rotations defining the kinematic poses to the reduced space of positions and velocities defined by the degrees of freedom of the articulated joints. This introduces a small but measurable loss.

  • 2.

    Sim2sim transfer. To take advantage of GPU-accelerated training, our Playgorund pipeline involves transferring controllers trained in an MJX-based simulation to a MuJoCo C-based simulation. These two MuJoCo versions handle contacts differently and operate on different hardware, potentially introducing noise and behavioral differences. We therefore tuned parameters across implementations manually to minimize these effects. As shown in Figure 3, any remaining differences are now negligible (see Sections 2.2.1 and the supplementary appendix A for additional details on the mitigation process).

  • 3.

    Simulation environment. Finally, the playground pipeline involves transferring the controllers from a Python-based to a Unity3D-based environment. The underlying engine is in both cases MuJoCo C, so theoretically there shouldn’t be a difference, but the codebase is still different and any discrepancy could lead to different results. Figure 3 shows that this difference is negligible, but it was significant during the process of establishing the processing pipeline and debugging the controller policies. We believe it is important to monitor this and any other possible source of difference.

    • 3.3 Comparing policies

    Table 2 summarizes the values of the animation fidelity index for each controller and animation reference rendered in Unity3D. To compare different training policies, we performed Wilcoxon paired tests, taking p<0.01 as a threshold for a significant difference. All training policies have scores significantly different (p<0.0001) from the reference (which has by construction a score of 1 for any animation).

    The comparison of DReCon and DeepMimic policies implemented in modular-agents confirms that, everything else being equal, having explicit information of the targeted pose at every frame produces better movement than only receiving rewards on movement similarity (mean difference 0.038,p<0.001). This comes, of course, at the cost of having to load and process the animation data at the inference stage.

    The comparison of DeepMimic policies trained in modular-agents and playground suggests that, everything else being equal, the playground pipeline gives equivalent results in terms of animation fidelity (mean difference 0.018,p=0.27). This suggests that the faster GPU pipeline enabling 100M+ environment steps in minutes does not sacrifice quality.

    In this regard, where DReCon has the best score of the modular-agents controllers, DeepMimic outscores all other playground controllers (AMP shows a mean difference of 0.143,p<0.0001; ADD shows a mean difference of 0.058,p=0.0021). If we focus only on playground controllers, we observe that ADD is a clear improvement over AMP (mean difference of 0.085,p<0.0001), but still does not match DeepMimic (mean difference 0.038,p=0.0042). Other metrics lead to similar conclusions. In supplementary section B, we show that the more common mean absolute joint-angle error (MAE) leads to similar conclusions when comparing playground policies.

    3.4 Visual inspection

    We complemented the quantitative metrics with expert feedback for the best playground policies (i.e. DeepMimic and ADD). The professional animator who retargeted and cleaned the animations (co-author [removed for submission anonymity]) did a systematic review comparing the animations in Motion Builder, with the controller policies in the web-based environment. In supplementary section C, a detailed breakdown can be found for each animation used to train the playground policies DeepMimic and ADD.

    Even the best policies moved too much the chest, which also made the arms and the head move more than in the reference animation. Sometimes the policy introduced jolts towards the sides, as well as exaggerated movements, which then had implications for the arms and the head. We believe that this is due to the policy training for stability -i.e., not falling-, but the phenomenon is found across policies, and we have not found a systematic way to fix it.

    This result may have appeared previously in the PBCA literature, but it may be less apparent due to the use of simpler skeletons (particularly with less joints on the spine), and to not using rigged and textured characters.

    4 Discussion

    4.1 Losses in retargeting

    The automated FBX-to-MJCF pipeline successfully produced training-ready ragdolls for both the adult male (MM) and female child (LL) skeletons, despite their significantly different proportions. The key step was the retargeting: the IK-based retargeting we used preserved end-effector positions well, but may have introduced artifacts in the torso chain—particularly for the LL skeleton. To map skeleton poses to the reduced space of the physical ragdoll, we still did automated retargeting, as have done virtually all recent contributions to PBCA.

    An alternative strategy, specific to our use case, could be to calculate the qPos and qVel needed to train the physical controllers simply using finite differences and joint constraints. This would only be reliable and precise because of the match between the skeleton poses and the ragdoll topology and it could, possibly, further reduce the fidelity loss introduced by the retargeting, even if it our results suggest it was already quite small.

    4.2 Sim to sim transfer

    Transferring controllers from MuJoCo-MJX to MuJoCo C introduced a measurable but small fidelity gap. This is analogous to the sim-to-real transfer challenges documented in robotics [11, 29], and our observation-design approach complements the domain randomization strategies typically used in that context [28]. We had expected this to be the main source of degradation in the MJX-based pipeline, but our results suggest that, in the final implementation of our playground pipeline, the degradation was minimal. The critical mitigation strategy was excluding simulator-specific observations (composite inertia tensors) from the policy input. The small remaining gap was probably dominated by differences in how collisions are handled, which affect contact-rich phases of the gait cycle.

    4.3 Controller losses

    The main animation fidelity loss was introduced in the training step. It could be argued that this was due to the constraint of having physically possible movements. However, we took all possible steps to preserve the animation of physical movements (creating characters matching the proportions of the actors, minimal editing of the animation). We also chose to work with walking motions because they do not involve too many physical contacts, and can easily be created in different styles. The different controller policies varied in the movement quality they produce, but the results of DeepMimic and ADD do suggest that there is a general threshold that physical controller policies do not manage to breach.

    4.4 Physics-based controllers for production

    We found that showing the result on rigged and textured characters is important to judge the quality of the motion generated by controller policies, but we could not find any article in the PBCA literature where the poses produced by the controller policy are directly mapped on a rigged and textured character. The recent MotionBricks [34] integrated controller policies in Unreal Engine, but the mapping to a rigged and textured character was done with retargeting and inverse kinematics, which did not allow validating the motion quality produced by the controller policies independently of the rest of the processing steps. It should also be pointed that MotionBricks also joins a growing amount of work [19, 18, 20, 14, 16] where the datasets and infrastructure needed for training the controller policies go largely beyond what is available in a typical VR production. This makes it difficult to adopt these controller policies for VR production.

    After inspecting the controller policies applied on rigged and textured characters, we believe there remains a fundamental gap in animation fidelity that is not solved with current policies. This animation fidelity gap is hard to detect with the most commonly used success metrics, but we could readily identify it comparing side by side the reference animation used for training and the movement generated by the policies trained, particularly when using animations with minimal physical constraints, like the walking cycles we used. For visual comparison, the deployment of the controllers in the VR-compatible web environment was very useful, and we’ve made it available together with the training pipeline.888 The source code of the web environment used is included in the supplementary materials and can also be found in [link removed for submission anonymity].

    The ceiling of the afi scores on the playground policies, which stayed far lower from the afi scores after retargeting, might also reflect this animation fidelity gap. In figure 3, it can be seen in the main afi score loss for playground policies, which occurs at the training stage, even before transferring to MuJoCo C. Further evaluation with improved policies should validate whether the ceiling found in afi scores really reflects the limits in animation fidelity found through visual inspection.

    Overall, we believe this gap is a fundamental challenge caused by the way these policies are trained: at the early stages of training the trials where the character does not fall produce a longer training episode, and therefore higher rewards. The strong movements of the chest help considerably to keep balance, and are therefore learnt early, even if these movements are not found in the reference animation. As the training progresses, the imitation rewards of DeepMimic and the adversarial comparison of AMP and ADD progressively bring the movement closer to the reference, but they do not overwrite these early learnt movements. The elimination of simulator-specific observations, such as inertia tensors, might have been good for transferring policies from MJX to MuJoCo C, but it might also contribute to this gap.

    5 Conclusions and future work

    Adversarial controllers like ADD provide results close to methods requiring explicit pose tracking (DReCon) or explicitly tracking the phase of an animation (DeepMimic), which encourages exploration of their use in production projects involving richer interactive behavior. However, they struggle with very asymmetric movements (like the Wounded animation, where the ADD policy fails to move forward in both characters). A possible solution is to introduce complementary rewards to compensate for such problems, and doing so specifically for challenging animations.

    When motion quality is an important goal, we recommend matching ragdoll and skeleton proportions and showing the result on rigged and textured characters, with a one-to-one retargeting of the ragdoll controller to the rigged and textured character, rather than ragdoll visualizations alone. Visual inspection is significantly more sensitive to movement errors on rigged and textured characters—subtle artifacts in joint velocities, foot skating, and phase shifts that are invisible on a ragdoll become immediately apparent on a rigged and textured mesh (see also supplementary video). This practice would help raise the bar for animation quality in physics-based control research. In addition, rendering PBCA controllers in WebXR can give animation fidelity results comparable to rendering them in a Unity3D environment. Moreover, doing so is very useful for a visual comparison of the movement generated by the policy and the reference animation. We recommend adopting systematic visual comparison with these tools. The metrics commonly used in the physics-based literature do not capture movement anomalies that an animation expert can readily detect. We recommend complementing any objective metric with expert assessment.

    Systematically assessing animation fidelity at different stages of transferring the controller to the final environment is necessary to detect quality losses. This includes not only the well explored sim2sim or sim2real transfer challenge, but also any retargeting and change of the environment where the simulation is run. This may help to improve movement quality, but also to understand why challenging tasks, involving rich contacts or complex interactions, are not learnt effectively. For the reference motion, if any motion retargeting is needed, manual methods are highly recommended.

    Despite all these considerations, we could not reliably generate physics-based controller policies for VR characters matching the quality of the reference animation. The behavior generated by the trained policies does allow identifying the reference motion, but even the best training methods induce the controller to move much more the chest than in the reference animation. There remains a significant gap between the reference animation and the movement generated by the controller policy. We believe this gap is difficult to close because of the way the controller policies are trained.

    Future work should explore alternative training strategies resulting in PBCA policies that bridge this animation fidelity gap and generate movement closer to the reference animation data. We would also like to complement this work by extending the evaluation to motions involving richer contacts and object interaction [35], and to integrate multi-motion universal controllers [28, 18, 31] into the comparison.

    This document accompanies the main paper “Animation fidelity in physics-based humanoid controllers”. It collects architecture and training decisions, additional animation-fidelity discussion, and complementary analyses.

    Appendix A Architecture and training decisions

    A significant effort of this work has been finding the right combination of software packages that enable seemless transfer from an MJX training pipeline to a Unity3D-based inference. Figure 4 shows a high-level architecture of the two pipelines and how we collected per-frame poses of the controller to compare with the reference motion.

    However, this does not show specific software package choices. We chose ONNX runtime because the default package to load ONNX models in Unity3D (Sentis) has practical differences in implementation that make the resulting control actions quite different. Therefore, only a port of ONNX Runtime enabled appropriate inference.999 Sentis and ONNX Runtime may diverge on the order of 10⁻² per output dimension, which the neural network controller will probably amplify.

    More generally, we selected MuJoCo playground over IsaacGym or IsaacLab for two reasons: (i) MuJoCo playground shares its physics engine with the MuJoCo C runtime used in our Unity3D deployment efforts (via the Unity3D mujoco-unity plugin), so the sim-to-sim gap reduces to numerical (CPU vs. XLA on GPU) rather than algorithmic differences in contact resolution; (ii) MuJoCo playground uses MJX, which is fully JAX-traceable, which lets us co-locate the environment, the PPO update, and the discriminator (for AMP/ADD) under a single jit boundary. The trade-off is that asset import in MJX is currently more restrictive than IsaacLab’s USD pipeline, which is why we author skeletons in MJCF and convert to Unity3D at deployment time rather than the reverse.

    For modular agents, we used a stable PD with a controller action every two steps. For MJX training, we used traditional PD controllers. This simplified transfer. However, we found that having slightly less frequent controller updates reduced jitter. We therefore chose to use control updates every 4 steps.
    One practical consequence of the 4-substep control window is that the reference trajectory must be re-sampled to the 31 Hz control rate before training, which truncates the original 120 Hz motion capture acquisition frequency to the nearest multiple of four substeps. Depending on the duration of the animation loop, this can imply drops ≤4 frames at the seam—small in absolute terms, but enough to introduce a sub-frame discontinuity that AMP’s discriminator amplifies. Future work should resample the reference inside the environment with a continuous-time interpolant rather than at asset-loading time, which would remove the seam artefact and, possibly, could improve AMP.

    AMP is particularly sensitive to the quality of the reference motion data: loop-seam discontinuities in the reference cause the discriminator to learn from physically impossible velocity spikes, and near-static motions (e.g., a subtle limp) cause temporal aliasing where the discriminator cannot form a meaningful decision boundary. Both failure modes can be addressed through hybrid reward (combining a small explicit tracking component with the adversarial objective), confirming the findings of Li et al. [15] that explicit rewards complement adversarial methods.

一句话：一篇真正的工程复盘：绕开官方通道，用引擎直出的 MV 与 depth 驱动末端神经渲染，再叠 SR。

要点：

  • 把它讲清楚的位置：DLSS 5 是**3D 引导的神经渲染**，作为图形管线的最终渲染阶段——引擎照常渲染几何/纹理/光照，末端用 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的部分（皮肤次散射、发丝与植被透光、接触阴影、GI）；DLSS 2→5 的走向是从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」
  • 工程现实很硬：硬件门槛是 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core（RTX 40/30/20 不支持，非 50 系创建 feature 18 直接返回 `0xBAD00001 FeatureNotSupported`）；SDK 截至 2026-10-07 未公开，Streamline 2.14.1 不含 DLSS NR，官方 UE 插件 v8.8.0 仍只到 DLSS 4.5
  • 所以社区路线是「直接调 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）」：他们用引擎直出的**运动矢量与深度**（不用光流估计，避免拖影），把 x_nr.dll 接进 UE5，IsaacSim 走 CUDA 后端，在不改物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下与 DLSS SR 叠加运行；作者也给出了自己的算力口径与后续自训 DiT 的计划

为什么值得看：这是国内少见的、把「官方通道缺位时怎么在引擎里跑通神经渲染」写清楚的复盘：参数（154M 骨架、FP8/FP16 混用）、实测延迟、报错码、集成路径、以及「引擎真值 MV/depth 优于光流估计」这条结论，都是可以直接拿去做技术判断的信息。

中文摘要：这篇复盘讲的是把 DLSS 5 接进仿真系统（UE5 与 IsaacSim）的完整工程路径。先给定位：DLSS 5 被官方定义为 3D 引导神经渲染，处在图形管线的最终渲染阶段——传统引擎照常渲染几何、纹理与光照，末端由 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的细节，如皮肤次表面散射、发丝与植被透光、接触阴影与 GI；代际演进的走向则是从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」。接着是硬约束：需要 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core，非 50 系创建 feature 18 会返回 0xBAD00001；SDK 尚未公开，Streamline 与官方 UE 插件都还没跟上。于是社区直接调用 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）：用引擎直出的运动矢量与深度替代光流估计，把模型接进 UE5，IsaacSim 走 CUDA 后端，在不改动物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下与 DLSS SR 叠加运行，并给出了参数量、延迟与显存口径以及自训 DiT 的后续计划。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：知乎（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-16

本话题属于超前点映，在官版生态完成前会持续更新。

2026 年 3 月底，NVIDIA 宣布了自研闭源 DLSS 5 技术，开启了游戏级神经渲染的时代。

我们做了个开箱即用的插件，应用到了仿真系统中去，IA Lab内部研究（SR+NR SDG ）：​HTTPS://www.k2sim.cn/reports/dlssnr-report/cabin_comparison.HTML

00:01 IsaacSim Warehouse NR capture / @IA Lab UnrealEngine5 NR capture @IA Lab DLSS 5 的成神之路：从超分到 3D 引导神经渲染

DLSS 5 被官方定义为 3D 引导神经渲染，为画面加入逼真光照与材质，并由开发者针对每款游戏调校最终输出 [6]；官方把它定位为图形管线的最终渲染阶段——传统引擎照常渲染几何、纹理、光照，DLSS 5 在末端用 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的细节，例如皮肤次表面散射、头发与植被透光、接触阴影、GI。

这种务实的思路与现在很多所谓“世界模型仿真”是完全相反的，给整个仿真体系带来了清晰的发展路径。

一代目到四代目：各代到底解决了什么

DLSS 从来不是单一功能。NVIDIA 对它的原始定义是神经图形技术：用 AI 成倍提升性能、生成全新帧、并通过图像重建显示更高分辨率 [1]。对不熟悉这条线的读者，一句话概括各代解决的问题：DLSS 2 解决「低分辨率渲染、高分辨率显示」；DLSS 3 解决「帧率不够」；DLSS 4 解决「模型架构换代」；DLSS 4.5 解决「帧生成与重建模型的进一步细化」；DLSS 5 解决「画面外观不够像照片」。

DLSS 2 之前，业界主要靠空间超分（比如各种插值算法）把低分辨率画面拉大，效果是糊；时间超分要跨帧累积信息，就必须知道每个像素上一帧在哪——这就是运动矢量（Motion Vector，每像素相对前帧的移动）的作用。没有准确的 MV，跨帧对齐就会错，画面就会拖影。DLSS 2.0 的输入管线里就已经有 Motion Vectors（R16G16_SFLOAT，每像素相对前帧的移动，不含 jitter 偏移）——这条输入约定一直沿用到今天。DLSS 4 用 Vision Transformer 替代所有 DLSS 功能（SR、RR、DLAA）中的 CNN，是图形行业中 transformer 的首个实时应用。DLSS 4.5 引入 Dynamic Multi Frame Generation，以及用于超分与光线重建的第二代 transformer 模型 [7]；第二代模型进一步改善稳定性、抗锯齿与视觉清晰度 [8]，光线重建侧则提升了光照准确性与响应、运动中的清晰度以及时间稳定性 [9]。

这条线的走向很清楚：从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」。DLSS 5 与 SR、MFG、RR 相互独立、可叠加，输入质量越高输出越好——我们可以看到明显的技术演进路径。

神经渲染为什么又快又好：单步像素空间扩散 Transformer

screen space motion vector就是像素移动的速度(v_x , v_y)，是所谓的temporal history的核心。

简单讲，我要渲染当前帧的图像(RGB -NR)，需要输入的是当前的无滤镜无美颜引擎直出的RGB（SceneColor），最好不要AA，不要多余的后处理。一帧进来，一帧出去。关你什么光照材质ABCD,一个大力滤镜干上去就完了。

那为啥还要像素单位的 Motion Vectors呢？其实是为了拿到blend 重采样之后的上一帧的RGB图，它隐含了历史渲染帧的信息，有效避免了闪烁和推理不稳定，位于模型的lane7-9位置。

世界先验：它强在哪，边界在哪

为什么能“变得真实”，核心就是这个小东西，有「外观先验」。它被教会了“这个材质的物体看上去应该是这样的”。本质上，网络学到的是「照片看起来是什么样」的统计分布，作用方式是在引擎渲染好的画面上把外观推向该分布，albedo、法线、光照在训练期做一致性监督，结果同时受作者意图约束。

世界模型应该明白这些事情，但是大多数都显得过于发散了，可控性很差。3D 引导在DLSS中承担对齐与稳定的大任，终究还是没有脱离渲染引擎啊。

社区版本是通过深度和光流信息估计来传数据到模型的，但是我们这里本身就能从引擎里拿到真值，所以路径会简单可靠的多。渲染内容相比自然视频的核心优势也在这里：精确的运动矢量和深度缓冲直接由引擎提供，无需通过光流估计来近似。这是它比通用视频生成模型更适合仿真域增强的根本原因。

玩家拒绝延迟：极简架构与算力口径

骨架约 154M 参数，多数 GEMM 与注意力用 FP8、少数数值敏感项用 FP16，相对 FP16 约 2×，为 Blackwell 与 TMA 指令优化。研究版推理约 8 ms / 3840×2160 帧（RTX 5090），峰值显存 731 MB，与游戏共享 GPU；这是研究版口径。第三方实测口径不同：固定开销 8.2–13.7 ms、帧率损失 40–60%。

相比于Cosmos等慢悠悠的世界模型，风格迁移，DLSS简直是一道闪电。

我们接进了仿真引擎中 官方通道还没开，社区先跑通了。其实，老黄自己都没想到大家这么喜欢这个东西。 硬件门槛是这条路径的硬约束。3D 引导神经渲染依赖 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core [10]；按官方兼容性表，RTX 40/30/20 均不支持 [11]。对已有 RTX 40 集群的团队，这不是「升级驱动」能解决的问题。 官方通道的可得性决定了工程路径。DLSS 5 于 2026-09-03/04 随 NBA 2K27 首发，RTX 50 独占（09-04 松口称将扩至 RTX 40）；UE5 插件存在（UE 5.8）但按工作室门槛发放。SDK 截至 2026-10-07 仍未公开发布，官方页面无下载或申请入口，Streamline 最新 2.14.1 不含 DLSS NR；官方 UE 插件更新至 v8.8.0，支持 UE 5.5–5.8，但仍仅 DLSS 4.5，无 DLSS 5。Omniverse/Kit/Isaac Sim 无任何 DLSS 5 支持，Kit 109 RTX 渲染器只有 SR/RR/FG。 官方通道缺位期间，社区跑通并被证明有效的方案集中在两类。第一类是引擎 hook 替换与直跑：UE5 游戏与编辑器自带官方 DLSS 插件提供的 hook，社区用 ReShade 配合 renodx 在 hook 上把 feature 换成 18，不需要 Feeder 式的合约合成，使 UE5 成为当前社区落地最顺的目标；OptiScaler 的 DLSSNR 分支可脱离 ReShade 直跑 NR，DLSS5-Swapper 则能自动定位 UE 引擎目录下的 NGX DLL。第二类是独立进程与离线批处理：DLSS5-Feeder 验证了「sidecar 进程 + 合成 DLAA 合约 + 私有 D3D12 device」的实时注入模式，ComfyUI-DLSS5-Enhancer 把 NGX feature 18 封装成图像序列与视频的离线批处理节点。两类方案共同指向一个结论：直接调用 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）是当下唯一稳定有效的底层通路。 无效通路与陈旧策略只需两句：Streamline 2.14.0 虽已新增 sl.dlss_nr 插件，但社区实测 Streamline 新加入的 sl.dlss_nr 插件仍不可用；而在拿不到引擎真值时靠着色器光流估计合成 MV 的外部注入策略容易产生拖影，拥有引擎源码时直取真值 MV 与 depth 即可规避。NGX 创建 feature 18 会做代际检查，非 RTX 50 返回 0xBAD00001 FeatureNotSupported。以上是 2026 年 10 月初的状态，官方口径是 2026 秋向开发者开放。

（声明，仅作研究测试）

简单来说，它对于我们来说，不是一个拿来就用的东西，主要面临的问题包括但不限于：

1）dll 逆向拿到所有可控有效参数，拿到dll里的模型权重，做好hash校验，

2）Linux移植与异构集群问题，目前官方只支持Windows Blackwell(5090) 615以上驱动，我们自己搭建了推理节点。

3）性能保持，即使是搞了多年性能优化的开发，也遇到了大量的坑。

4）和已有采集方案的兼容性。isaacsim 其实底层设计的问题蛮多，UE5 - IADATASDG我们自己的系统就容易得多。虽然如此，现代渲染全部都是异步+多线，错综交杂的资源队列，真的看的头疼。

除了模型没训，其他的都拆开重组了一遍。

虽然这个过程中遇到了一点点坑，我们还是通过 NGX 等将 x_nr.dll 模型接进了 UE5 ， Isaacsim 则是用cuda后端来搭载——在不改动物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下，直接用引擎产出的色彩、运动矢量与深度驱动末端神经渲染，并与 DLSS SR 叠加运行。

实际画面表现可以直接看实机 2K SR / NR 同帧对比交互展示页（涵盖 Original 2K、DLSS SR、NR 2K 与 NR + SR 四种变体及像素擦除对比）：

点击查看：HTTPS://www.k2sim.cn/reports/dlssnr-report/cabin_comparison.HTML

我们计划训练自己的 DiT

把 NGX 接入跑通只是第一步。虽然 NVIDIA 原厂的 158MB 闭源权重本身不可直接拆改，但参考 DLSS 5 的实现思路，自己训练一个面向仿真域的像素空间 DiT 模型在技术上是可行的演进方向。

为什么可行？一是从建模范式看，G-buffer 到最终真实感图像的映射本质上就是条件图像生成问题，用扩散模型替代 GAN 规避了模式坍缩与训练不稳定性；ControlNet 已经证明可以在不破坏生成先验的前提下注入精确的空间控制条件；单步像素空间扩散的理论与训练路径也已有公开研究可供参考。

二是从数据壁垒看，仿真引擎恰恰握有训练这类模型最稀缺的资产。相比自然视频必须靠光流估计去猜运动，引擎天然逐帧产出精确的运动矢量、深度与 G-buffer 真值；同时，合成数据生产本身正在往自动采集、标注、质检并形成可追踪数据版本的方向演进 [12]，仿真农场可以持续生成「实时光栅化 + G-buffer ↔ 路径追踪 / 真实采集」的成对数据。方法论并不神秘，真正的壁垒在于高质量成对数据与工程管线积累；而自研 DiT 一旦跑通，有望摆脱对特定代际硬件的依赖，并能针对无人机巡检、具身抓取等特定传感器与光照分布做定向增强。

如果风格控制的路径可达，那么理论上我们可以1个场景->n个风格渲染。

这给我们什么启示：神经网络会遍布仿真引擎全身吗

不会取代物理与几何管线，而是以「3D 条件引导的末端外观重建层」成为仿真引擎的标准组件。 早先 Intel ISL 的 G-buffer 条件 Sim2Real 方案在 RTX 3090 上只有 2 FPS 且局限于特定街景，而 DLSS 5 通过单步扩散与 FP8 Tensor Core 把同一思路推进到了 4K 实时。几何、材质、动力学仍然由引擎和物理求解器保证精确性，神经网络落在它们之后，在像素空间里弥合成像域的分布差距。

把这条路线放进仿真生产链路，只需要守住两条验证红线：

  1. 多视角一致性：单视角独立增强可能幻觉出跨视角不一致的纹理，直接用于 3DGS 三维重建有致命风险，作为感知训练域增强也必须经过闭环 A/B 验证；
  2. 几何与标签一致性：增强必须精确保留输入的几何结构与语义边界（在合成数据采集中可将 Tone Intensity 置零以保留原始帧色彩分布），同时清醒认识到「人眼看着更像照片」只代表感知真实度提升，不等于更接近渲染器定义的物理辐射参考。

欢迎感兴趣的朋友和我们的研究员一起聊聊，留言或者私信都会回复，神经动力学也将会是我们研究的一个重要方向，期待不久后和各位读者相见。

一句话：一篇真正的工程复盘：绕开官方通道，用引擎直出的 MV 与 depth 驱动末端神经渲染，再叠 SR。

要点：

  • 把它讲清楚的位置：DLSS 5 是**3D 引导的神经渲染**，作为图形管线的最终渲染阶段——引擎照常渲染几何/纹理/光照，末端用 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的部分（皮肤次散射、发丝与植被透光、接触阴影、GI）；DLSS 2→5 的走向是从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」
  • 工程现实很硬：硬件门槛是 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core（RTX 40/30/20 不支持，非 50 系创建 feature 18 直接返回 `0xBAD00001 FeatureNotSupported`）；SDK 截至 2026-10-07 未公开，Streamline 2.14.1 不含 DLSS NR，官方 UE 插件 v8.8.0 仍只到 DLSS 4.5
  • 所以社区路线是「直接调 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）」：他们用引擎直出的**运动矢量与深度**（不用光流估计，避免拖影），把 x_nr.dll 接进 UE5，IsaacSim 走 CUDA 后端，在不改物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下与 DLSS SR 叠加运行；作者也给出了自己的算力口径与后续自训 DiT 的计划

为什么值得看：这是国内少见的、把「官方通道缺位时怎么在引擎里跑通神经渲染」写清楚的复盘：参数（154M 骨架、FP8/FP16 混用）、实测延迟、报错码、集成路径、以及「引擎真值 MV/depth 优于光流估计」这条结论，都是可以直接拿去做技术判断的信息。

中文摘要：这篇复盘讲的是把 DLSS 5 接进仿真系统（UE5 与 IsaacSim）的完整工程路径。先给定位：DLSS 5 被官方定义为 3D 引导神经渲染，处在图形管线的最终渲染阶段——传统引擎照常渲染几何、纹理与光照，末端由 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的细节，如皮肤次表面散射、发丝与植被透光、接触阴影与 GI；代际演进的走向则是从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」。接着是硬约束：需要 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core，非 50 系创建 feature 18 会返回 0xBAD00001；SDK 尚未公开，Streamline 与官方 UE 插件都还没跟上。于是社区直接调用 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）：用引擎直出的运动矢量与深度替代光流估计，把模型接进 UE5，IsaacSim 走 CUDA 后端，在不改动物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下与 DLSS SR 叠加运行，并给出了参数量、延迟与显存口径以及自训 DiT 的后续计划。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：知乎（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-11-16

本话题属于超前点映，在官版生态完成前会持续更新。

2026 年 3 月底，NVIDIA 宣布了自研闭源 DLSS 5 技术，开启了游戏级神经渲染的时代。

我们做了个开箱即用的插件，应用到了仿真系统中去，IA Lab内部研究（SR+NR SDG ）：​HTTPS://www.k2sim.cn/reports/dlssnr-report/cabin_comparison.HTML

00:01 IsaacSim Warehouse NR capture / @IA Lab UnrealEngine5 NR capture @IA Lab DLSS 5 的成神之路：从超分到 3D 引导神经渲染

DLSS 5 被官方定义为 3D 引导神经渲染，为画面加入逼真光照与材质，并由开发者针对每款游戏调校最终输出 [6]；官方把它定位为图形管线的最终渲染阶段——传统引擎照常渲染几何、纹理、光照，DLSS 5 在末端用 AI 补上实时渲染被迫省略的细节，例如皮肤次表面散射、头发与植被透光、接触阴影、GI。

这种务实的思路与现在很多所谓“世界模型仿真”是完全相反的，给整个仿真体系带来了清晰的发展路径。

一代目到四代目：各代到底解决了什么

DLSS 从来不是单一功能。NVIDIA 对它的原始定义是神经图形技术：用 AI 成倍提升性能、生成全新帧、并通过图像重建显示更高分辨率 [1]。对不熟悉这条线的读者，一句话概括各代解决的问题：DLSS 2 解决「低分辨率渲染、高分辨率显示」；DLSS 3 解决「帧率不够」；DLSS 4 解决「模型架构换代」；DLSS 4.5 解决「帧生成与重建模型的进一步细化」；DLSS 5 解决「画面外观不够像照片」。

DLSS 2 之前，业界主要靠空间超分（比如各种插值算法）把低分辨率画面拉大，效果是糊；时间超分要跨帧累积信息，就必须知道每个像素上一帧在哪——这就是运动矢量（Motion Vector，每像素相对前帧的移动）的作用。没有准确的 MV，跨帧对齐就会错，画面就会拖影。DLSS 2.0 的输入管线里就已经有 Motion Vectors（R16G16_SFLOAT，每像素相对前帧的移动，不含 jitter 偏移）——这条输入约定一直沿用到今天。DLSS 4 用 Vision Transformer 替代所有 DLSS 功能（SR、RR、DLAA）中的 CNN，是图形行业中 transformer 的首个实时应用。DLSS 4.5 引入 Dynamic Multi Frame Generation，以及用于超分与光线重建的第二代 transformer 模型 [7]；第二代模型进一步改善稳定性、抗锯齿与视觉清晰度 [8]，光线重建侧则提升了光照准确性与响应、运动中的清晰度以及时间稳定性 [9]。

这条线的走向很清楚：从「重建分辨率」到「重建光线」再到「重建外观」。DLSS 5 与 SR、MFG、RR 相互独立、可叠加，输入质量越高输出越好——我们可以看到明显的技术演进路径。

神经渲染为什么又快又好：单步像素空间扩散 Transformer

screen space motion vector就是像素移动的速度(v_x , v_y)，是所谓的temporal history的核心。

简单讲，我要渲染当前帧的图像(RGB -NR)，需要输入的是当前的无滤镜无美颜引擎直出的RGB（SceneColor），最好不要AA，不要多余的后处理。一帧进来，一帧出去。关你什么光照材质ABCD,一个大力滤镜干上去就完了。

那为啥还要像素单位的 Motion Vectors呢？其实是为了拿到blend 重采样之后的上一帧的RGB图，它隐含了历史渲染帧的信息，有效避免了闪烁和推理不稳定，位于模型的lane7-9位置。

世界先验：它强在哪，边界在哪

为什么能“变得真实”，核心就是这个小东西，有「外观先验」。它被教会了“这个材质的物体看上去应该是这样的”。本质上，网络学到的是「照片看起来是什么样」的统计分布，作用方式是在引擎渲染好的画面上把外观推向该分布，albedo、法线、光照在训练期做一致性监督，结果同时受作者意图约束。

世界模型应该明白这些事情，但是大多数都显得过于发散了，可控性很差。3D 引导在DLSS中承担对齐与稳定的大任，终究还是没有脱离渲染引擎啊。

社区版本是通过深度和光流信息估计来传数据到模型的，但是我们这里本身就能从引擎里拿到真值，所以路径会简单可靠的多。渲染内容相比自然视频的核心优势也在这里：精确的运动矢量和深度缓冲直接由引擎提供，无需通过光流估计来近似。这是它比通用视频生成模型更适合仿真域增强的根本原因。

玩家拒绝延迟：极简架构与算力口径

骨架约 154M 参数，多数 GEMM 与注意力用 FP8、少数数值敏感项用 FP16，相对 FP16 约 2×，为 Blackwell 与 TMA 指令优化。研究版推理约 8 ms / 3840×2160 帧（RTX 5090），峰值显存 731 MB，与游戏共享 GPU；这是研究版口径。第三方实测口径不同：固定开销 8.2–13.7 ms、帧率损失 40–60%。

相比于Cosmos等慢悠悠的世界模型，风格迁移，DLSS简直是一道闪电。

我们接进了仿真引擎中 官方通道还没开，社区先跑通了。其实，老黄自己都没想到大家这么喜欢这个东西。 硬件门槛是这条路径的硬约束。3D 引导神经渲染依赖 RTX 50 系与第五代 Tensor Core [10]；按官方兼容性表，RTX 40/30/20 均不支持 [11]。对已有 RTX 40 集群的团队，这不是「升级驱动」能解决的问题。 官方通道的可得性决定了工程路径。DLSS 5 于 2026-09-03/04 随 NBA 2K27 首发，RTX 50 独占（09-04 松口称将扩至 RTX 40）；UE5 插件存在（UE 5.8）但按工作室门槛发放。SDK 截至 2026-10-07 仍未公开发布，官方页面无下载或申请入口，Streamline 最新 2.14.1 不含 DLSS NR；官方 UE 插件更新至 v8.8.0，支持 UE 5.5–5.8，但仍仅 DLSS 4.5，无 DLSS 5。Omniverse/Kit/Isaac Sim 无任何 DLSS 5 支持，Kit 109 RTX 渲染器只有 SR/RR/FG。 官方通道缺位期间，社区跑通并被证明有效的方案集中在两类。第一类是引擎 hook 替换与直跑：UE5 游戏与编辑器自带官方 DLSS 插件提供的 hook，社区用 ReShade 配合 renodx 在 hook 上把 feature 换成 18，不需要 Feeder 式的合约合成，使 UE5 成为当前社区落地最顺的目标；OptiScaler 的 DLSSNR 分支可脱离 ReShade 直跑 NR，DLSS5-Swapper 则能自动定位 UE 引擎目录下的 NGX DLL。第二类是独立进程与离线批处理：DLSS5-Feeder 验证了「sidecar 进程 + 合成 DLAA 合约 + 私有 D3D12 device」的实时注入模式，ComfyUI-DLSS5-Enhancer 把 NGX feature 18 封装成图像序列与视频的离线批处理节点。两类方案共同指向一个结论：直接调用 NGX 的 D3D12 API（feature 18）是当下唯一稳定有效的底层通路。 无效通路与陈旧策略只需两句：Streamline 2.14.0 虽已新增 sl.dlss_nr 插件，但社区实测 Streamline 新加入的 sl.dlss_nr 插件仍不可用；而在拿不到引擎真值时靠着色器光流估计合成 MV 的外部注入策略容易产生拖影，拥有引擎源码时直取真值 MV 与 depth 即可规避。NGX 创建 feature 18 会做代际检查，非 RTX 50 返回 0xBAD00001 FeatureNotSupported。以上是 2026 年 10 月初的状态，官方口径是 2026 秋向开发者开放。

（声明，仅作研究测试）

简单来说，它对于我们来说，不是一个拿来就用的东西，主要面临的问题包括但不限于：

1）dll 逆向拿到所有可控有效参数，拿到dll里的模型权重，做好hash校验，

2）Linux移植与异构集群问题，目前官方只支持Windows Blackwell(5090) 615以上驱动，我们自己搭建了推理节点。

3）性能保持，即使是搞了多年性能优化的开发，也遇到了大量的坑。

4）和已有采集方案的兼容性。isaacsim 其实底层设计的问题蛮多，UE5 - IADATASDG我们自己的系统就容易得多。虽然如此，现代渲染全部都是异步+多线，错综交杂的资源队列，真的看的头疼。

除了模型没训，其他的都拆开重组了一遍。

虽然这个过程中遇到了一点点坑，我们还是通过 NGX 等将 x_nr.dll 模型接进了 UE5 ， Isaacsim 则是用cuda后端来搭载——在不改动物理仿真与上游几何管线的前提下，直接用引擎产出的色彩、运动矢量与深度驱动末端神经渲染，并与 DLSS SR 叠加运行。

实际画面表现可以直接看实机 2K SR / NR 同帧对比交互展示页（涵盖 Original 2K、DLSS SR、NR 2K 与 NR + SR 四种变体及像素擦除对比）：

点击查看：HTTPS://www.k2sim.cn/reports/dlssnr-report/cabin_comparison.HTML

我们计划训练自己的 DiT

把 NGX 接入跑通只是第一步。虽然 NVIDIA 原厂的 158MB 闭源权重本身不可直接拆改，但参考 DLSS 5 的实现思路，自己训练一个面向仿真域的像素空间 DiT 模型在技术上是可行的演进方向。

为什么可行？一是从建模范式看，G-buffer 到最终真实感图像的映射本质上就是条件图像生成问题，用扩散模型替代 GAN 规避了模式坍缩与训练不稳定性；ControlNet 已经证明可以在不破坏生成先验的前提下注入精确的空间控制条件；单步像素空间扩散的理论与训练路径也已有公开研究可供参考。

二是从数据壁垒看，仿真引擎恰恰握有训练这类模型最稀缺的资产。相比自然视频必须靠光流估计去猜运动，引擎天然逐帧产出精确的运动矢量、深度与 G-buffer 真值；同时，合成数据生产本身正在往自动采集、标注、质检并形成可追踪数据版本的方向演进 [12]，仿真农场可以持续生成「实时光栅化 + G-buffer ↔ 路径追踪 / 真实采集」的成对数据。方法论并不神秘，真正的壁垒在于高质量成对数据与工程管线积累；而自研 DiT 一旦跑通，有望摆脱对特定代际硬件的依赖，并能针对无人机巡检、具身抓取等特定传感器与光照分布做定向增强。

如果风格控制的路径可达，那么理论上我们可以1个场景->n个风格渲染。

这给我们什么启示：神经网络会遍布仿真引擎全身吗

不会取代物理与几何管线，而是以「3D 条件引导的末端外观重建层」成为仿真引擎的标准组件。 早先 Intel ISL 的 G-buffer 条件 Sim2Real 方案在 RTX 3090 上只有 2 FPS 且局限于特定街景，而 DLSS 5 通过单步扩散与 FP8 Tensor Core 把同一思路推进到了 4K 实时。几何、材质、动力学仍然由引擎和物理求解器保证精确性，神经网络落在它们之后，在像素空间里弥合成像域的分布差距。

把这条路线放进仿真生产链路，只需要守住两条验证红线：

  1. 多视角一致性：单视角独立增强可能幻觉出跨视角不一致的纹理，直接用于 3DGS 三维重建有致命风险，作为感知训练域增强也必须经过闭环 A/B 验证；
  2. 几何与标签一致性：增强必须精确保留输入的几何结构与语义边界（在合成数据采集中可将 Tone Intensity 置零以保留原始帧色彩分布），同时清醒认识到「人眼看着更像照片」只代表感知真实度提升，不等于更接近渲染器定义的物理辐射参考。

item.description:
一句话：三件套（帧生成/超分/光线重建）对标 DLSS 全家桶，目标是不锁厂商。

要点：

  • 模块划分直接对标现有生态：**ANR FG**（帧生成，已 beta）、**ANR SR**（超分，beta 将至）、**ANR RR**（光线追踪降噪/光线重建，beta 将至）
  • 安装方式说明它面向既有游戏而非新引擎：`anr-fg-full` 给没用 OptiScaler 的游戏，`anr-fg-addon` 给已经用 OptiScaler 的游戏；Windows 走 `install.cmd`，Linux/Steam Deck 用 `WINEDLLOVERRIDES="dxgi=n,b"` 或 `winmm=n,b`
  • 仓库里还带了 **nr-record**：录制游戏的帧生成/上采样输入，用来横向比较 ANR FG 与 DLSS-G、DLSS、FSR、XeSS 等方案——这是一份可直接拿来复现对比的工具

Apex Neural Rendering (ANR)

Apex Neural Rendering by Apex Compute.

  • ANR FG: frame generation. In beta.
  • ANR SR: super resolution (upscaling). Beta soon.
  • ANR RR: ray reconstruction (denoising for ray tracing). Beta soon.
  • Source code: coming soon.
  • nr-record: records a game's frame generation or upscaler inputs to compare ANR FG, NVIDIA DLSS-G, DLSS, FSR, XeSS and others (below). Source in this repository.

    • ANR FG Beta

  • Download a package from Releases: 
  • anr-fg-full
    : for games without OptiScaler.
  • anr-fg-addon
    : for games that already use OptiScaler.
  • Close the game, extract the package and run the installer with the folder of the game's 
    .exe
    :
  • Windows: 
    install.cmd
  • Linux and Steam Deck (Proton): 
    sh install.sh ""
    , then set the game's launch options to the line it prints: 
    WINEDLLOVERRIDES="dxgi=n,b" %command%
    , or 
    winmm=n,b
    in Vulkan games
  • In the game, turn on frame generation (the NVIDIA option where the game offers several).

    • To uninstall, run 

    uninstall.cmd
    or 
    sh uninstall.sh
    with the same folder.

    Supported GPUs

  • NVIDIA GeForce RTX 20, 30, 40 and 50 series, and GTX 16 series
  • AMD Radeon RX 5000, 6000, 7000 and 9000 series, and Steam Deck
  • Intel Arc A and B series

    • On Windows 10 and 11, and on Linux and SteamOS with Proton.

    Results and problems

    Please post them as issues:

  • Performance results: run the test kit from the release and attach its result file.
  • Problems: the game, GPU and driver, operating system, settings and what you saw, with the newest 
    nr_fg-*.log
    from under the game's 
    OptiScaler/custom/Apex Neural Rendering FG
    folder.

    • OptiScaler is GPL-3.0; its source for each release is attached to the release.

    Record and compare frame generation

    nr-record records the inputs a game gives its frame generation, losslessly. You can then replay a recording through any frame generation DLL you have (ANR FG, a game's DLSS-G 

    nvngx_dlssg.dll
    ) and compare the results as videos or images. nr-record includes no frame generation.

    Requirements:

  • a D3D12 or Vulkan game with DLSS frame generation, with the 
    anr-fg-full
    package installed (it includes OptiScaler);
  • Windows 10 or 11, or Linux with Proton;
  • ffmpeg and ffprobe on the 
    PATH
    ;
  • for DLSS-G replays, an NVIDIA RTX 40 or 50 series GPU.

  • Install. Download 

    nr-record-1.2-windows.zip
    or 
    nr-record-1.2-linux.tar.gz
    from the FG-V.B18 release and extract it. Close the game and run the installer with the folder of the game's 
    .exe
    :

  • Windows: 
    install.cmd ""
    . No launch option is needed.
  • Linux and Steam Deck (Proton): 
    sh install.sh ""
    . Set the game's Steam launch options to 
    WINEDLLOVERRIDES="dxgi=n,b" %command%
    (the ANR FG installer prints the same line). Do not set this on Windows: the game may not start.

    • The installer copies 

    nr-record
    into 
    OptiScaler/custom/
    and sets 
    FGNvngxReplacement=nr-record
    in 
    OptiScaler.ini
    (it keeps the original). When you are not recording, ANR FG generates the frames, or DLSS-G if ANR FG is not installed (
    forward
    in 
    nr-record/dlssg/nr_record.ini
    ). 
    uninstall.cmd
    or 
    sh uninstall.sh
    with the same folder removes nr-record and restores 
    OptiScaler.ini
    . To install by hand: copy 
    capture/OptiScaler/custom/nr-record
    into 
    OptiScaler/custom/
    , set 
    FGNvngxReplacement=nr-record
    , and set 
    forward
    to 
    ..\..\Apex Neural Rendering FG\dlssg\nvngx_dlssg.dll
    or 
    nvidia
    .

  • Record. Turn on DLSS frame generation in the game. F6 starts and stops a recording; F9 records the next 8 frames. Each start and stop beeps. While recording, the game shows only real frames. Recordings go to 

    %LOCALAPPDATA%\nr-record\
    (Windows) or 
    ~/.local/share/nr-record/
    (Proton). A frame takes about 26 MB at 3840x2160 and 6 MB at 1806x972. 
    nr-record/dlssg/nr_record--.log
    lists what was recorded.

    To record the upscaler's inputs instead (super resolution, D3D12 games): open OptiScaler's menu (Insert), pick 

    nr-record
    in the upscaler list, and press F6 to start and stop. It upscales with the upscaler 
    OptiScaler.ini
    names (DLSS on NVIDIA, else FSR, or XeSS) and records that output too. Pick your upscaler again afterwards. Replay these recordings with 
    --generator dlss
    , 
    fsr
    or 
    xess
    (replay).

  • Replay. On Windows, in the package folder (

    REC
    is a recording's folder):

    tools\nr-record.exe info REC
tools\nr-replay.exe --record REC --out out\anr --generator provider --dll "\nvngx_dlssg.dll" --label "ANR FG" --stream - | tools\nr-video.exe video - --out out\anr.mp4
tools\nr-replay.exe --record REC --out out\dlssg --generator nvidia --dll "\nvngx_dlssg.dll" --label DLSS-G --stream - | tools\nr-video.exe video - --out out\dlssg.mp4
tools\nr-video.exe project out\anr.mp4 out\dlssg.mp4 --out out\cmp.compare.json --labels "ANR FG" DLSS-G

    On Linux, one command runs both replays under Proton's Wine and writes both videos, a side-by-side video and the compare project:

    python3 tools/nr_replay_wine.py --record REC --out cmp --video \
    --generator provider --dll "/nvngx_dlssg.dll" --label "ANR FG" \
    --b-generator nvidia --b-dll "/nvngx_dlssg.dll" --b-label DLSS-G

    For images, replay with 

    --raw
    instead of 
    --stream
    and run 
    nr-video png
    .

  • Compare.

    viewer/renderer --compare --project cmp/compare.json
    (Windows: 
    viewer\renderer.exe --compare --project out\cmp.compare.json
    ) plays both videos in sync, with a divider, side by side view, pixel zoom and marks, and exports videos and images. From the command line: 
    --compare-export PROJECT --out FILE --very-high
    . 
    viewer/renderer --captures
    lists your recordings and regenerates their frames with each generator.

    • Docs: recording, format, replay and videos, viewer.

    Build: 

    bazel build //record:nr-record //record/replay:nr-video //renderer
    ; Windows parts: 
    bazel build --config=windows_cross //record/capture:package //record/replay:nr-replay
    .

    Citation

  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://github.com/apex-compute/ANR},
  note   = {https://apexcompute.com/neural-rendering}
}
