item.title: 把手机随手拍变成电影感：FilmTogether 要同时升级光照、服装与材质，但不动构图、身份与运动 ｜ FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
item.description:
一句话：不换人脸、不换运镜，只把「低成本」的那几项制作要素补上。

要点：

  • 任务定义很清楚：要弥合随手拍与高成本电影制作之间的美学落差，必须升级**异质的制作要素**（光照、专用服装、材质），同时不改动原素材的构图、身份与时序运动
  • 两个瓶颈被点名：一是缺少专门针对「复杂低→高外观迁移」的高质量配对训练数据；二是现有视频编辑模型没有充分利用它对多种低成本线索的感知能力
  • FilmTogether 因此针对这两点设计，而不是笼统地做「视频风格化」

为什么值得看：「只改该改的」是内容管线里最实用的约束：不能换脸、不能动运镜，否则素材就废了。把光照/服装/材质当作可独立升级的要素，比端到端重绘更接近真实的美术流程。

中文摘要：移动设备普及让录制变得廉价，但随手拍与高成本电影制作之间仍存在明显的美学落差。要弥合它，就必须升级那些异质的制作要素——光照、专用服装、材质等——同时保持原素材的构图、身份与时序运动不变。这条任务被两个瓶颈卡住：一是缺少专门面向「复杂低到高外观迁移」的高质量配对训练数据；二是现有视频编辑模型没有充分发挥其对多种低成本线索的感知能力。FilmTogether 针对这两点设计，目标不是笼统的视频风格化，而是可控地补齐「制作规格」这一层，因此更接近真实内容管线里「只改该改的」这件事。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-10-31

本期推送：2026-11-16

FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation
from Low-Cost Inputs

Abstract

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.

Code & Data: FilmTogether  · CineCraft-120K

1 Introduction

The rapid evolution of mobile technology has made video recording accessible to everyone, fundamentally changing how everyday moments are captured and shared. However, a persistent visual gap remains between these casual, low-cost videos and professional cinematic productions. Low-cost videos are typically characterized by amateur framing, ordinary settings, and suboptimal lighting, whereas high-cost productions benefit from professional equipment, sophisticated illumination, and intricate set designs. Advances in denoising, latent, video, and transformer-based diffusion models [18, 37, 38, 36, 19, 33] have propelled instruction-based video editing to new heights [11, 46, 2], yet transforming a basic low-cost video into a cinematic masterpiece remains a largely unexplored frontier. Bridging this aesthetic divide is not a simple global style transfer, but it requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements—such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials—without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage.

Realizing this low-to-high cost transformation is heavily bottlenecked by two primary challenges: 1) Lacking high-quality paired training data for complex appearance shifts. The progress of specialized cinematic editing is hampered by the scarcity of appropriate training data. Current video editing datasets often emphasize generic instructions or broad stylization [49, 15, 21]. They lack the domain-specific mappings and task diversity required to supervise the intricate transition from low-cost to high-cost aesthetics while strictly preserving spatial layout and motion. There is a distinct absence of large-scale, paired data that explicitly captures these element-level production upgrades. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current models to better perceive and enhance multiple low-cost compositions. At the model level, existing architectures struggle to strengthen the heterogeneous and multiple low-cost compositions. Standard generators (e.g., Ditto [2]) typically inject source visual hints directly into a frozen denoising backbone, leaving the model with limited capacity to process semantic instructions related to complex appearance changes, and failing to reliably disentangle the core structure from the low-cost aesthetic.

In this work, we present CineCraft-120K, a carefully curated, high-quality dataset comprising over 120K premium cinematic video clips, with over 99% of the clips feature a resolution of at least 1080p and are accompanied by detailed captions. As shown in Fig. 1 and 2, our CineCraft-120K has several characteristics: 1). Superior visual diversity and temporal coverage: The cinematic crafting bank distinguishes itself through exceptional visual diversity, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories, while encompassing over five decades of media production from 1970 to 2023. This extensive temporal coverage prevents the model from overfitting to contemporary trends, ensuring it learns generalized and enduring cinematic aesthetics. 2). High-quality video pairs via a scalable dataset pipeline: Supported by approximately 1,500 GPU days computational source, it features over 120K high-resolution, aligned low- and high-cost video pairs generated through a highly efficient, automated construction pipeline. Through strict multi-dimensional quality filtering, this intensive approach ensures superior visual richness and clarity, with over 99% of the resulting cinematic clips featuring 1080p or 4K resolutions. 3). Expressive in pair-aware rich textual captions: Unlike datasets that provide generic video descriptions, it introduces highly detailed, pair-aware element-wise prompts averaging around 125 dense words. These expressive instructions are grounded in the actual visual transformations between counterparts, precisely detailing coordinated upgrades to heterogeneous elements like lighting, color grading, and materials.

To address the architecture deficit, we propose a dual-memory adapter that seamlessly maps low-cost inputs to cinematic quality with minimal overhead. At the semantic level, the Instruction-Routed Text Memory expands the instruction representation capacity via learnable text-memory token, overcoming the limitations of global textual prompts in detailing diverse production elements. In parallel, the Layer-Wise Hint Memory operates at the visual context injection to supply layer-specific corrections to the source video hints before DiT fusion. This adaptive feature refinement prevents the generative process from being bottlenecked by the coarse textures and defects of the source video, enabling multi-level enhancements from low-level aesthetics to high-level layouts. Synergistically, the text memory deeply enriches the cinematic semantics while the hint memory finely calibrates the visual context, facilitating sophisticated element-level upgrades with high efficiency.

Our contributions are listed as follows: 1). We introduce CineCraft-120K, a large-scale, high-quality dataset comprising over 120K aligned low- and high-cost video pairs with pair-aware prompts for cinematic video editing. 2). We propose a Dual-Memory Adapter, which combines text and layer-wise hint memories to seamlessly execute complex aesthetic transformations with minimal overhead. 3). We design a VLM-Aesthetic evaluator and demonstrate the superiority of our framework on the low-to-high-cost video editing task.

2 CineCraft-120K: Paired Cinematic Data Construction

We introduce CineCraft-120K, a large-scale paired dataset for upgrading low-cost videos into cinematic productions while preserving their underlying scene structure and motion. Its construction follows three design principles: diverse cinematic scenarios, structure-preserving counterpart synthesis, and pair-aware, element-level instruction caption annotations. Starting from a curated high-cost visual bank, we synthesize low-cost counterparts and subsequently annotate the reverse transformation through precise comparison of each video pair. This approach retains real cinematic footage as the enhancement target while providing explicit supervision for coordinated changes to heterogeneous production elements. Fig. 1 illustrates the complete pipeline.

2.1 Cinematic Videos Curation and Pair-Aware Data Construction

Diverse Cinematic Source Collection. To capture a broad range of cinematic appearances, we collect visually rich footage from films, television series, and crawled open-world videos. The source collection spans media released between 1970 and 2023 and is organized into five broad visual domains and 23 fine-grained categories. This coverage exposes the dataset to varied production designs, lighting styles, costumes, and materials across genres and eras, broadening its scope beyond contemporary cinematic appearances. The crawled subset further extends the collection to visual content beyond narrative film and television.

Shot-Coherent Preprocessing. We first remove openings, endings, black bars, subtitle regions, and other non-content areas using manually specified temporal boundaries and spatial crops. We then apply adaptive shot detection with PySceneDetect[7] to obtain temporally coherent clips without crossing detected shot boundaries. Clips shorter than 4 seconds are discarded; those between 4 and 6 seconds are retained; those longer than 6 but shorter than 8 seconds are truncated to their first 6 seconds; and those of at least 8 seconds are evenly divided into approximately 4–6-second segments. This procedure produces compact source clips while avoiding short residual segments and preserving within-shot continuity.

Multi-Dimensional Quality Curation. We combine manual screening for visually rich, high-production-value content with automated perceptual quality filtering. VBench [22] evaluates aesthetic and imaging quality, for which we reject the bottom 15% and 20% of candidates, respectively. FineVQ [13] provides complementary blur- and noise-related quality assessments, with the lowest-quality 15% rejected under each criterion. A clip is removed if it falls into the rejection set of any criterion. This filtering strategy screens for complementary failure modes, including weak composition, exposure and distortion artifacts, excessive noise, and blurred details. The retained clips form the high-cost visual bank that supplies cinematic targets for subsequent pair construction.

Structure-Guided High-to-Low Synthesis. To construct paired supervision, we generate a low-cost counterpart for each selected high-cost clip by simplifying its production-related appearance under structural guidance. From each reference clip, we extract the first frame and estimate a depth sequence using Video-Depth-Anything [9]. Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct [4] examines the first frame and generates a high-to-low editing instruction that identifies visually elaborate elements and specifies replacements while retaining their spatial arrangement. Qwen-Image-Edit [44], implemented through DiffSynth-Studio, applies this instruction to produce a low-cost first frame. Wan2.1-VACE-14B [23, 42] then synthesizes the low-cost video conditioned on the edited frame and reference depth sequence. The edited frame establishes the intended low-cost appearance, while the depth sequence guides scene geometry and temporal motion. The overall construction effort uses approximately 1,500 GPU-days. This process supports large-scale pair generation with appearance changes guided by a shared underlying scene structure.

Prompt-Guided Verification and Adaptive Annotation. We use the preceding high-to-low editing instruction as a reference to verify whether the synthesized low-cost video realizes the intended appearance changes. Specifically, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct jointly examines the editing instruction, the original high-cost video, and its generated low-cost counterpart to assess whether the specified element-level modifications are reflected in the resulting pair. This comparison identifies discrepancies between the intended and realized edits, including changes that are missing, only partially achieved, or introduced beyond the instruction.

When discrepancies are detected, the instruction is adaptively revised to reflect the transformations actually observed in the video pair. The verified and adjusted transformation description is then expressed as a low-to-high enhancement instruction, specifying how to upgrade the generated low-cost video toward its high-cost reference. This verification-and-adaptation process grounds the final supervision in both the original editing intent and the realized visual changes, reducing mismatches between textual instructions and paired video content.

2.2 Dataset Characteristics: Diversity, Quality, and Expressiveness

We characterize CineCraft-120K through visual coverage, source quality, and pair-aware instructions. Its high-cost bank contains 124,902 clips totaling 176.38 hours; Figures 2 and 3 summarize its statistics.

Visual Diversity and Historical Coverage. CineCraft-120K spans 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained categories. The taxonomy covers Chinese costume and historical scenes (7 categories), sci-fi and speculative content (5), Western fantasy (3), European aristocratic scenes, and crawled open-world content (7), from wuxia and palace settings to space opera and epic landscapes (Fig. 2(a)).

Sources span 1970–2023, while crawled clips extend beyond film and television. Their largest visual groups are nature/epic scenes (23.4%), sci-fi/technology/VFX (18.8%), cinematic mood (14.2%), and action/vehicles (13.0%); the remaining groups are fantasy/royalty (11.9%), crowds/events (10.3%), and people/fashion (8.5%) (Figs. 2(b) and 3(b)).

Large-Scale, High-Quality Cinematic Paired Videos. Television contributes about 76% of the visual bank, and 99% of source clips are 1080p or 4K. Combined with multi-dimensional quality filtering, these sources provide detailed appearance references; Fig. 3(a) shows their frame-count distribution.

Expressive, Pair-Aware Editing Captions. Prompt-guided verification grounds each low-to-high instruction in the edits realized by its video pair. Instructions average 124.7 words (median 122; IQR 108–138) and describe coordinated changes to lighting, color, clothing, materials, and scene appearance. Their length and vocabulary distributions appear in Figs. 3(c,d).

3 Methodology: Dual-Memory Adaptation

Given a low-cost source video and an editing instruction, FilmTogether aims to enhance cinematic appearance while preserving source identity, spatial layout, and temporal motion. This task requires coordinated changes to heterogeneous production elements, including illumination, costumes, materials, and set design. It therefore places complementary demands on the conditioning pathways: textual features must represent the intended appearance changes, while visual features must retain structural guidance without restricting generation to the source appearance.

FilmTogether builds on Wan2.1-VACE-14B [42, 23].

As shown in Fig. 4, we introduce a dual-memory adapter that augments both conditioning pathways while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen.

Instruction-Routed Text Memory supplements the instruction with learnable, adaptively gated tokens.

Layer-Wise Hint Memory uses the augmented instruction to retrieve layer-specific residuals that refine source-video hints before their injection into the transformer-based DiT Main Branch [41, 33].

Instruction-Routed Text Memory. The frozen text encoder provides general-purpose instruction features but cannot directly adapt its parameters to cinematic enhancement. We introduce a learnable memory that expands the conditioning representation while retaining the original instruction tokens.

For clarity, let C=[c₁,…,c_L]∈ℝ^B×L×d_T denote the frozen text-encoder features and c̄=L⁻¹∑ᵢcᵢ their pooled representation. The learnable text-memory codes are Mᵀ={mᵀₖ}ₖ₌₁^K (K=4), each with the same dimension as a text token. A lightweight router predicts independent sigmoid gates:

(1)

where c̄ is the mean-pooled instruction feature, LN is layer normalization [1], φ is GELU [16], sigmoid independently maps each router logit to [0,1], W₁ᵀ and W₂ᵀ are the trainable Text-Router projections, k indexes a memory code, and the superscript T denotes Text Memory. The gates scale the codes before appending them to the original text sequence:

C̃=[C;aᵀ₁mᵀ₁;…;aᵀ_Kmᵀ_K].

(2)

where C̃∈ℝ^B×(L+K)×d_T is the augmented instruction sequence, B is the batch size, L is the instruction length, d_T is the text-feature dimension, cᵢ∈ℝ^d_T is the i-th frozen text token, K=4 is the number of learnable codes, mₖᵀ∈ℝ^d_T is the k-th code, [ ; ] denotes token-wise concatenation.

Independently gated memory tokens expand semantic capacity for coordinated appearance upgrades while retaining the original instruction tokens. Unlike softmax selection, the independent gates can activate several codes simultaneously for instructions that combine lighting, material, costume, and set-design changes, while appending the codes preserves every literal instruction token.

Layer-Wise Hint Memory. The VACE Context Branch extracts source-video hints {H_ℓ} at designated fusion locations. These features carry structural information useful for preserving the source, but may also encode its low-cost textures, lighting, and other appearance characteristics. Hint Memory introduces an instruction-conditioned residual at each fusion location, allowing the visual conditioning to adapt before entering the main branch.

π^H=softmax (W^H₂ φ (W^H₁LN(Pool(P(C̃))))), ∑ₖ₌₁^Kπₖ^H=1.

(3)

where P is the frozen projection from text width d_T to the DiT hidden width, Pool averages the projected tokens, W₁^H and W₂^H are the trainable Hint-Router projections, π^H=[π₁^H,…,π_K^H] is the resulting instruction-conditioned distribution, and the superscript H denotes Hint Memory. Each fusion location ℓ owns an independent bank M_ℓ^H={m^H_ℓ,k}ₖ₌₁^K in the DiT hidden dimension. The shared routing decision reads a layer-specific correction:

Δh_ℓ=∑ₖ₌₁^Kπₖ^Hm^H_ℓ,k.

where ℓ indexes a DiT fusion location, m_ℓ,k^H is the k-th code in that bank, πₖ^H is its shared instruction-dependent weight, and Δh_ℓ is the resulting layer-specific correction.

Here the correction is broadcast to all hint tokens. Independent token banks let early, middle, and late fusion locations learn different corrections. Its interaction with position-dependent features and subsequent attention yields non-uniform spatiotemporal effects. Placing the correction before fusion is important, after considering the fact that the original hint continues to anchor identity, geometry, and motion, while the routed residual removes the need for the main branch to inherit its low-cost appearance unchanged. Layer-specific token banks further allow early injections to refine local texture and illumination and later injections to adjust higher-level scene organization, without unfreezing the visual backbone.

Distilled Aesthetic Evaluator. Following knowledge distillation [17], we distill Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview’s aesthetic assessments of 5,000 edited clips into Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking [3] using LoRA [20] and token-level cross-entropy loss. Supervision includes five aspect scores, an overall score, and corresponding rationales. Used only for evaluation, the frozen model receives edited frames and weak instruction context. We report its overall score as VLM-Aesthetic; Appendix B.1 provides the full rubric.

4 Experiments and Results

4.1 Experimental Setup

Implementation details. Our model builds on Wan2.1-VACE-14B [42, 23] with Ditto’s Context-Branch LoRA [2]. We augment the pretrained editor with Text Memory and layer-wise Hint Memory, then fine-tune on the CineCraft-120K training split. The reference-frame prior is linearly annealed and disabled at inference. We use AdamW [30] with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ and weight decay of 0.01. Both stages use bfloat16 and an effective batch size of eight.

Competitors. We compare Filmtogether against VACE [23], Bernini-R-14B [39], Ditto [2], InsV2V [11], InsViE [46], TokenFlow [14], ICVE [27], Kiwi-Edit [28], SANA-Streaming [48], Señorita [49], ReCo [47], and Lucy-Edit [40]. For a fair comparison, we evaluate each baseline using the settings recommended in its paper or official implementation.

Evaluation metrics. We measure temporal consistency using CLIP-F [35] and DINO-F [6], which compute mean adjacent-frame feature cosine similarity, and text-conditioned preference using frame-averaged PickScore [25]. For cinematic quality, we use the VLM-Aesthetic evaluator detailed in Appendix B.1 to deterministically score two edited frames sampled at 1 fps and resized to 640 pixels wide. We report its holistic score, a semantic-design score averaging narrative/emotional fit, style/world consistency, and composition/lighting, and separate color/texture and hierarchy/readability scores.

Cinematic Crafting Benchmark (CineCraft-Bench). CineCraft-Bench comprises 100 videos spanning Chinese costume and historical scenes, science fiction, Western fantasy, European aristocratic settings, and open-world content. These videos cover diverse subjects, environments, and cinematic styles, with editing instructions targeting lighting, color grading, costumes, materials, and scene appearance.

4.2 Quantitative Comparison

Table 1 compares FilmTogether with 12 state-of-the-art video editing models on low-to-high-cost cinematic enhancement. FilmTogether achieves the highest CLIP-F (0.9967) and DINO-F (0.9985), indicating strong temporal consistency during appearance transformation. Its VLM-Aesthetic score is 3.87, compared with 3.77 for Bernini-R-14B.

The fine-grained aesthetic scores further highlight its effectiveness for low-to-high enhancement. FilmTogether leads in narrative/style/lighting (3.88), color/texture (3.86), and hierarchy/readability (3.91), respectively. These results support its ability to coordinate improvements across multiple production elements while maintaining temporally consistent outputs. Overall, the results demonstrate the method’s strength in cinematic appearance enhancement and temporal consistency, the two complementary requirements of low-to-high-cost video editing.

4.3 Qualitative Comparison

We inspect representative results under matched inputs and instructions. Figure 5 presents two representative cases and exposes the trade-off between edit strength and source preservation. VACE often under-edits, while stronger baselines can alter faces or scene layout. FilmTogether introduces period-specific portrait cues and futuristic holographic panels and smoke while retaining identity, pose, and viewpoint across frames, yielding controlled enhancement rather than unconstrained redrawing. Additional examples of cinematic editing on everyday basketball and piano videos are provided in Appendix B.2.

4.4 Dataset Ablation

The paired CineCraft-120K data improves VLM-Aesthetic from 3.22 to 3.78 for Ditto and from 3.66 to 3.87 for FilmTogether, while also improving temporal and fine-grained appearance scores (Table 2).

4.5 User Study

User Study Protocol. Ten participants compare FilmTogether with Ditto and Bernini-R-14B on ten randomly selected low-to-high editing cases. For each case, they view the source video, editing instruction, and three synchronized outputs with anonymized method labels. Case order is randomized across participants, and output positions vary across cases. Participants select one preferred output for each of six criteria: instruction following, cinematic enhancement, content preservation, motion fidelity, temporal consistency, and visual quality and realism, yielding 600 selections in total and 100 per criterion. We report selection rates for each criterion and their unweighted mean.

Human Preference Results. Figure 6 shows that FilmTogether achieves the highest observed selection rate across all six criteria, averaging 74.3%, compared with 21.2% for Bernini-R-14B and 4.5% for Ditto. It receives 72% of selections for cinematic enhancement, compared with 26% for Bernini-R-14B and 2% for Ditto. It also leads in content preservation (79%), motion fidelity (83%), temporal consistency (81%), and visual quality and realism (77%). The margin is smaller for instruction following (54% versus 43% for Bernini-R-14B). These results support FilmTogether’s perceived ability to enhance cinematic appearance while retaining source content and motion on the evaluated cases.

5 Conclusion

We present FilmTogether for transforming low-cost videos into cinematic outputs while preserving source content and motion. CineCraft-120K provides 23 diverse scenarios, aligned video pairs, and pair-aware editing instructions. Its dual-memory adapter coordinates semantic edits with layer-wise visual guidance. Quantitative results and human evaluation show improved cinematic appearance and temporal consistency, supporting accessible low-to-high video enhancement.

Appendix A Related Work

Video-to-video Datasets. Large-scale captioned video corpora and caption-transfer pipelines, including WebVid, VideoCC, Panda-70M, InternVid, and OpenVid-1M, support video-language pretraining but do not provide paired editing transformations [5, 31, 10, 43, 32]. InsV2V synthesizes video pairs from related prompts [11], whereas InsViE-1M, Ditto-1M, and FFP-300K use frame-guided editing and temporal propagation or synthesis [46, 2, 21]. Señorita-2M and OpenVE-3M employ specialist or category-specific pipelines for diverse editing operations [49, 15]. Appendix Table A1 summarizes the key characteristics of these approaches. Our CineCraft-120K specializes this strategy for cinematic enhancement, pairing curated high-production-value targets with synthesized low-cost counterparts and prompts grounded in observed differences. It focuses on coordinated upgrades to lighting, costumes, and materials while preserving scene structure and motion.

Instruction-based Video Editing. Diffusion-based video editors adapt image priors through one-shot tuning, zero-shot inversion and attention reuse, anchor-frame propagation, or flow-guided attention [45, 24, 34, 8, 29, 12]. AnyV2V instead combines an image editor with image-to-video propagation in a tuning-free pipeline [26]. Inversion-based methods such as TokenFlow [14] reuse source features and inter-frame correspondences under target text guidance, while paired-data methods such as InsV2V [11] and InsViE [46] learn instruction-driven transformations. FFP-300K [21] uses an edited first frame to specify the target appearance. Ditto’s Editto [2] bridges reference-guided training and instruction-driven inference by gradually removing this reference during training. OpenVE-Edit [15] further enriches conditioning through a video–instruction encoder and a task-aware MOE connector. Our dual-memory adapter augments text conditioning and refines layer-wise source hints within the existing editor, supporting cinematic instruction interpretation and low-cost appearance adaptation.

Appendix B Additional Experimental Details

B.1 Aesthetic Evaluator Details

Scoring rubric.

The teacher and distilled evaluator use a four-level rubric for every aspect: 4 denotes an excellent or strongly successful result, 3 a good result with minor issues, 2 a weak result with clear issues, and 1 a failed result or one that harms the intended aesthetic. The five aspects are defined as follows.

  • 1.

    Narrative and emotional fit: integration with scene mood, emotional tone, and visual context without distracting anomalies.

  • 2.

    Style and world consistency: compatibility with the era, genre, environment, and overall visual language.

  • 3.

    Composition and lighting design: composition, contrast, lighting hierarchy, lens design, and shot-level arrangement.

  • 4.

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-10-31

本期推送：2026-11-16

FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation
from Low-Cost Inputs

Abstract

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.

Code & Data: FilmTogether  · CineCraft-120K

1 Introduction

The rapid evolution of mobile technology has made video recording accessible to everyone, fundamentally changing how everyday moments are captured and shared. However, a persistent visual gap remains between these casual, low-cost videos and professional cinematic productions. Low-cost videos are typically characterized by amateur framing, ordinary settings, and suboptimal lighting, whereas high-cost productions benefit from professional equipment, sophisticated illumination, and intricate set designs. Advances in denoising, latent, video, and transformer-based diffusion models [18, 37, 38, 36, 19, 33] have propelled instruction-based video editing to new heights [11, 46, 2], yet transforming a basic low-cost video into a cinematic masterpiece remains a largely unexplored frontier. Bridging this aesthetic divide is not a simple global style transfer, but it requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements—such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials—without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage.

Realizing this low-to-high cost transformation is heavily bottlenecked by two primary challenges: 1) Lacking high-quality paired training data for complex appearance shifts. The progress of specialized cinematic editing is hampered by the scarcity of appropriate training data. Current video editing datasets often emphasize generic instructions or broad stylization [49, 15, 21]. They lack the domain-specific mappings and task diversity required to supervise the intricate transition from low-cost to high-cost aesthetics while strictly preserving spatial layout and motion. There is a distinct absence of large-scale, paired data that explicitly captures these element-level production upgrades. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current models to better perceive and enhance multiple low-cost compositions. At the model level, existing architectures struggle to strengthen the heterogeneous and multiple low-cost compositions. Standard generators (e.g., Ditto [2]) typically inject source visual hints directly into a frozen denoising backbone, leaving the model with limited capacity to process semantic instructions related to complex appearance changes, and failing to reliably disentangle the core structure from the low-cost aesthetic.

In this work, we present CineCraft-120K, a carefully curated, high-quality dataset comprising over 120K premium cinematic video clips, with over 99% of the clips feature a resolution of at least 1080p and are accompanied by detailed captions. As shown in Fig. 1 and 2, our CineCraft-120K has several characteristics: 1). Superior visual diversity and temporal coverage: The cinematic crafting bank distinguishes itself through exceptional visual diversity, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories, while encompassing over five decades of media production from 1970 to 2023. This extensive temporal coverage prevents the model from overfitting to contemporary trends, ensuring it learns generalized and enduring cinematic aesthetics. 2). High-quality video pairs via a scalable dataset pipeline: Supported by approximately 1,500 GPU days computational source, it features over 120K high-resolution, aligned low- and high-cost video pairs generated through a highly efficient, automated construction pipeline. Through strict multi-dimensional quality filtering, this intensive approach ensures superior visual richness and clarity, with over 99% of the resulting cinematic clips featuring 1080p or 4K resolutions. 3). Expressive in pair-aware rich textual captions: Unlike datasets that provide generic video descriptions, it introduces highly detailed, pair-aware element-wise prompts averaging around 125 dense words. These expressive instructions are grounded in the actual visual transformations between counterparts, precisely detailing coordinated upgrades to heterogeneous elements like lighting, color grading, and materials.

To address the architecture deficit, we propose a dual-memory adapter that seamlessly maps low-cost inputs to cinematic quality with minimal overhead. At the semantic level, the Instruction-Routed Text Memory expands the instruction representation capacity via learnable text-memory token, overcoming the limitations of global textual prompts in detailing diverse production elements. In parallel, the Layer-Wise Hint Memory operates at the visual context injection to supply layer-specific corrections to the source video hints before DiT fusion. This adaptive feature refinement prevents the generative process from being bottlenecked by the coarse textures and defects of the source video, enabling multi-level enhancements from low-level aesthetics to high-level layouts. Synergistically, the text memory deeply enriches the cinematic semantics while the hint memory finely calibrates the visual context, facilitating sophisticated element-level upgrades with high efficiency.

Our contributions are listed as follows: 1). We introduce CineCraft-120K, a large-scale, high-quality dataset comprising over 120K aligned low- and high-cost video pairs with pair-aware prompts for cinematic video editing. 2). We propose a Dual-Memory Adapter, which combines text and layer-wise hint memories to seamlessly execute complex aesthetic transformations with minimal overhead. 3). We design a VLM-Aesthetic evaluator and demonstrate the superiority of our framework on the low-to-high-cost video editing task.

2 CineCraft-120K: Paired Cinematic Data Construction

We introduce CineCraft-120K, a large-scale paired dataset for upgrading low-cost videos into cinematic productions while preserving their underlying scene structure and motion. Its construction follows three design principles: diverse cinematic scenarios, structure-preserving counterpart synthesis, and pair-aware, element-level instruction caption annotations. Starting from a curated high-cost visual bank, we synthesize low-cost counterparts and subsequently annotate the reverse transformation through precise comparison of each video pair. This approach retains real cinematic footage as the enhancement target while providing explicit supervision for coordinated changes to heterogeneous production elements. Fig. 1 illustrates the complete pipeline.

2.1 Cinematic Videos Curation and Pair-Aware Data Construction

Diverse Cinematic Source Collection. To capture a broad range of cinematic appearances, we collect visually rich footage from films, television series, and crawled open-world videos. The source collection spans media released between 1970 and 2023 and is organized into five broad visual domains and 23 fine-grained categories. This coverage exposes the dataset to varied production designs, lighting styles, costumes, and materials across genres and eras, broadening its scope beyond contemporary cinematic appearances. The crawled subset further extends the collection to visual content beyond narrative film and television.

Shot-Coherent Preprocessing. We first remove openings, endings, black bars, subtitle regions, and other non-content areas using manually specified temporal boundaries and spatial crops. We then apply adaptive shot detection with PySceneDetect[7] to obtain temporally coherent clips without crossing detected shot boundaries. Clips shorter than 4 seconds are discarded; those between 4 and 6 seconds are retained; those longer than 6 but shorter than 8 seconds are truncated to their first 6 seconds; and those of at least 8 seconds are evenly divided into approximately 4–6-second segments. This procedure produces compact source clips while avoiding short residual segments and preserving within-shot continuity.

Multi-Dimensional Quality Curation. We combine manual screening for visually rich, high-production-value content with automated perceptual quality filtering. VBench [22] evaluates aesthetic and imaging quality, for which we reject the bottom 15% and 20% of candidates, respectively. FineVQ [13] provides complementary blur- and noise-related quality assessments, with the lowest-quality 15% rejected under each criterion. A clip is removed if it falls into the rejection set of any criterion. This filtering strategy screens for complementary failure modes, including weak composition, exposure and distortion artifacts, excessive noise, and blurred details. The retained clips form the high-cost visual bank that supplies cinematic targets for subsequent pair construction.

Structure-Guided High-to-Low Synthesis. To construct paired supervision, we generate a low-cost counterpart for each selected high-cost clip by simplifying its production-related appearance under structural guidance. From each reference clip, we extract the first frame and estimate a depth sequence using Video-Depth-Anything [9]. Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct [4] examines the first frame and generates a high-to-low editing instruction that identifies visually elaborate elements and specifies replacements while retaining their spatial arrangement. Qwen-Image-Edit [44], implemented through DiffSynth-Studio, applies this instruction to produce a low-cost first frame. Wan2.1-VACE-14B [23, 42] then synthesizes the low-cost video conditioned on the edited frame and reference depth sequence. The edited frame establishes the intended low-cost appearance, while the depth sequence guides scene geometry and temporal motion. The overall construction effort uses approximately 1,500 GPU-days. This process supports large-scale pair generation with appearance changes guided by a shared underlying scene structure.

Prompt-Guided Verification and Adaptive Annotation. We use the preceding high-to-low editing instruction as a reference to verify whether the synthesized low-cost video realizes the intended appearance changes. Specifically, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct jointly examines the editing instruction, the original high-cost video, and its generated low-cost counterpart to assess whether the specified element-level modifications are reflected in the resulting pair. This comparison identifies discrepancies between the intended and realized edits, including changes that are missing, only partially achieved, or introduced beyond the instruction.

When discrepancies are detected, the instruction is adaptively revised to reflect the transformations actually observed in the video pair. The verified and adjusted transformation description is then expressed as a low-to-high enhancement instruction, specifying how to upgrade the generated low-cost video toward its high-cost reference. This verification-and-adaptation process grounds the final supervision in both the original editing intent and the realized visual changes, reducing mismatches between textual instructions and paired video content.

2.2 Dataset Characteristics: Diversity, Quality, and Expressiveness

We characterize CineCraft-120K through visual coverage, source quality, and pair-aware instructions. Its high-cost bank contains 124,902 clips totaling 176.38 hours; Figures 2 and 3 summarize its statistics.

Visual Diversity and Historical Coverage. CineCraft-120K spans 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained categories. The taxonomy covers Chinese costume and historical scenes (7 categories), sci-fi and speculative content (5), Western fantasy (3), European aristocratic scenes, and crawled open-world content (7), from wuxia and palace settings to space opera and epic landscapes (Fig. 2(a)).

Sources span 1970–2023, while crawled clips extend beyond film and television. Their largest visual groups are nature/epic scenes (23.4%), sci-fi/technology/VFX (18.8%), cinematic mood (14.2%), and action/vehicles (13.0%); the remaining groups are fantasy/royalty (11.9%), crowds/events (10.3%), and people/fashion (8.5%) (Figs. 2(b) and 3(b)).

Large-Scale, High-Quality Cinematic Paired Videos. Television contributes about 76% of the visual bank, and 99% of source clips are 1080p or 4K. Combined with multi-dimensional quality filtering, these sources provide detailed appearance references; Fig. 3(a) shows their frame-count distribution.

Expressive, Pair-Aware Editing Captions. Prompt-guided verification grounds each low-to-high instruction in the edits realized by its video pair. Instructions average 124.7 words (median 122; IQR 108–138) and describe coordinated changes to lighting, color, clothing, materials, and scene appearance. Their length and vocabulary distributions appear in Figs. 3(c,d).

3 Methodology: Dual-Memory Adaptation

Given a low-cost source video and an editing instruction, FilmTogether aims to enhance cinematic appearance while preserving source identity, spatial layout, and temporal motion. This task requires coordinated changes to heterogeneous production elements, including illumination, costumes, materials, and set design. It therefore places complementary demands on the conditioning pathways: textual features must represent the intended appearance changes, while visual features must retain structural guidance without restricting generation to the source appearance.

FilmTogether builds on Wan2.1-VACE-14B [42, 23].

As shown in Fig. 4, we introduce a dual-memory adapter that augments both conditioning pathways while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen.

Instruction-Routed Text Memory supplements the instruction with learnable, adaptively gated tokens.

Layer-Wise Hint Memory uses the augmented instruction to retrieve layer-specific residuals that refine source-video hints before their injection into the transformer-based DiT Main Branch [41, 33].

(1)

where c̄ is the mean-pooled instruction feature, LN is layer normalization [1], φ is GELU [16], sigmoid independently maps each router logit to [0,1], W₁ᵀ and W₂ᵀ are the trainable Text-Router projections, k indexes a memory code, and the superscript T denotes Text Memory. The gates scale the codes before appending them to the original text sequence:

(2)

Independently gated memory tokens expand semantic capacity for coordinated appearance upgrades while retaining the original instruction tokens. Unlike softmax selection, the independent gates can activate several codes simultaneously for instructions that combine lighting, material, costume, and set-design changes, while appending the codes preserves every literal instruction token.

These features carry structural information useful for preserving the source, but may also encode its low-cost textures, lighting, and other appearance characteristics. Hint Memory introduces an instruction-conditioned residual at each fusion location, allowing the visual conditioning to adapt before entering the main branch.

(3)

where P is the frozen projection from text width d_T to the DiT hidden width, Pool averages the projected tokens, W₁^H and W₂^H are the trainable Hint-Router projections, π^H=[π₁^H,…,π_K^H] is the resulting instruction-conditioned distribution, and the superscript H denotes Hint Memory. Each fusion location ℓ owns an independent bank M_ℓ^H={m^H_ℓ,k}ₖ₌₁^K in the DiT hidden dimension. The shared routing decision reads a layer-specific correction:

Here the correction is broadcast to all hint tokens. Independent token banks let early, middle, and late fusion locations learn different corrections. Its interaction with position-dependent features and subsequent attention yields non-uniform spatiotemporal effects. Placing the correction before fusion is important, after considering the fact that the original hint continues to anchor identity, geometry, and motion, while the routed residual removes the need for the main branch to inherit its low-cost appearance unchanged. Layer-specific token banks further allow early injections to refine local texture and illumination and later injections to adjust higher-level scene organization, without unfreezing the visual backbone.

Distilled Aesthetic Evaluator. Following knowledge distillation [17], we distill Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview’s aesthetic assessments of 5,000 edited clips into Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking [3] using LoRA [20] and token-level cross-entropy loss. Supervision includes five aspect scores, an overall score, and corresponding rationales. Used only for evaluation, the frozen model receives edited frames and weak instruction context. We report its overall score as VLM-Aesthetic; Appendix B.1 provides the full rubric.

4 Experiments and Results

4.1 Experimental Setup

Implementation details. Our model builds on Wan2.1-VACE-14B [42, 23] with Ditto’s Context-Branch LoRA [2]. We augment the pretrained editor with Text Memory and layer-wise Hint Memory, then fine-tune on the CineCraft-120K training split. The reference-frame prior is linearly annealed and disabled at inference. We use AdamW [30] with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ and weight decay of 0.01. Both stages use bfloat16 and an effective batch size of eight.

Competitors. We compare Filmtogether against VACE [23], Bernini-R-14B [39], Ditto [2], InsV2V [11], InsViE [46], TokenFlow [14], ICVE [27], Kiwi-Edit [28], SANA-Streaming [48], Señorita [49], ReCo [47], and Lucy-Edit [40]. For a fair comparison, we evaluate each baseline using the settings recommended in its paper or official implementation.

Evaluation metrics. We measure temporal consistency using CLIP-F [35] and DINO-F [6], which compute mean adjacent-frame feature cosine similarity, and text-conditioned preference using frame-averaged PickScore [25]. For cinematic quality, we use the VLM-Aesthetic evaluator detailed in Appendix B.1 to deterministically score two edited frames sampled at 1 fps and resized to 640 pixels wide. We report its holistic score, a semantic-design score averaging narrative/emotional fit, style/world consistency, and composition/lighting, and separate color/texture and hierarchy/readability scores.

Cinematic Crafting Benchmark (CineCraft-Bench). CineCraft-Bench comprises 100 videos spanning Chinese costume and historical scenes, science fiction, Western fantasy, European aristocratic settings, and open-world content. These videos cover diverse subjects, environments, and cinematic styles, with editing instructions targeting lighting, color grading, costumes, materials, and scene appearance.

4.2 Quantitative Comparison

Table 1 compares FilmTogether with 12 state-of-the-art video editing models on low-to-high-cost cinematic enhancement. FilmTogether achieves the highest CLIP-F (0.9967) and DINO-F (0.9985), indicating strong temporal consistency during appearance transformation. Its VLM-Aesthetic score is 3.87, compared with 3.77 for Bernini-R-14B.

The fine-grained aesthetic scores further highlight its effectiveness for low-to-high enhancement. FilmTogether leads in narrative/style/lighting (3.88), color/texture (3.86), and hierarchy/readability (3.91), respectively. These results support its ability to coordinate improvements across multiple production elements while maintaining temporally consistent outputs. Overall, the results demonstrate the method’s strength in cinematic appearance enhancement and temporal consistency, the two complementary requirements of low-to-high-cost video editing.

4.3 Qualitative Comparison

We inspect representative results under matched inputs and instructions. Figure 5 presents two representative cases and exposes the trade-off between edit strength and source preservation. VACE often under-edits, while stronger baselines can alter faces or scene layout. FilmTogether introduces period-specific portrait cues and futuristic holographic panels and smoke while retaining identity, pose, and viewpoint across frames, yielding controlled enhancement rather than unconstrained redrawing. Additional examples of cinematic editing on everyday basketball and piano videos are provided in Appendix B.2.

4.4 Dataset Ablation

The paired CineCraft-120K data improves VLM-Aesthetic from 3.22 to 3.78 for Ditto and from 3.66 to 3.87 for FilmTogether, while also improving temporal and fine-grained appearance scores (Table 2).

4.5 User Study

User Study Protocol. Ten participants compare FilmTogether with Ditto and Bernini-R-14B on ten randomly selected low-to-high editing cases. For each case, they view the source video, editing instruction, and three synchronized outputs with anonymized method labels. Case order is randomized across participants, and output positions vary across cases. Participants select one preferred output for each of six criteria: instruction following, cinematic enhancement, content preservation, motion fidelity, temporal consistency, and visual quality and realism, yielding 600 selections in total and 100 per criterion. We report selection rates for each criterion and their unweighted mean.

Human Preference Results. Figure 6 shows that FilmTogether achieves the highest observed selection rate across all six criteria, averaging 74.3%, compared with 21.2% for Bernini-R-14B and 4.5% for Ditto. It receives 72% of selections for cinematic enhancement, compared with 26% for Bernini-R-14B and 2% for Ditto. It also leads in content preservation (79%), motion fidelity (83%), temporal consistency (81%), and visual quality and realism (77%). The margin is smaller for instruction following (54% versus 43% for Bernini-R-14B). These results support FilmTogether’s perceived ability to enhance cinematic appearance while retaining source content and motion on the evaluated cases.

5 Conclusion

We present FilmTogether for transforming low-cost videos into cinematic outputs while preserving source content and motion. CineCraft-120K provides 23 diverse scenarios, aligned video pairs, and pair-aware editing instructions. Its dual-memory adapter coordinates semantic edits with layer-wise visual guidance. Quantitative results and human evaluation show improved cinematic appearance and temporal consistency, supporting accessible low-to-high video enhancement.

It focuses on coordinated upgrades to lighting, costumes, and materials while preserving scene structure and motion.

Diffusion-based video editors adapt image priors through one-shot tuning, zero-shot inversion and attention reuse, anchor-frame propagation, or flow-guided attention [45, 24, 34, 8, 29, 12].
